levels.title: Reading the record and producing the artifacts: disclosure items, contract clauses, public filings, tax-basis statements and the auditable deal packet

units.title: Reading what decides the deal: statutory disclosure items, contract clauses, public filings, tax-basis statements and conditional offers

lessons.title: Counting the items in a state disclosure: what an offer must say, and where the lists differ by jurisdiction
lessons.explanation: A disclosure document is not a summary of a deal. It is a list of statements that a statute requires a provider to make, and the only honest way to read it is to fetch the list from the statute and count against it, item by item, in the order the statute numbers them. Virginia's Chapter 22.1, Sales-Based Financing Providers, requires nine numbered disclosures at the time of extending a specific offer: (1) the total amount of the sales-based financing and the disbursement amount if it differs, after any fees deducted or withheld at disbursement; (2) the finance charge; (3) the total repayment amount, defined as the disbursement amount plus the finance charge; (4) the estimated number of payments, based on the projected sales volume, that equal the total repayment amount; (5) the payment amounts, which for fixed payments means the amounts, frequency and method and for variable payments means a schedule or a description of the method used to calculate the amounts and frequency and the payment method; (6) a description of all other potential fees and charges not included in the finance charge, naming draw fees, late payment fees, returned payment fees and prepayment fees or penalties; (7) if the recipient elects to pay off or refinance before full repayment, an updated disclosure of items 1 through 6 as of the day of prepayment or refinance plus a description of prepayment policies, including whether additional fees or penalties apply or whether a discount to the finance charge is given; (8) a description of collateral requirements or security interests; and (9) a statement of whether the provider will pay compensation directly to a broker in connection with that specific offer and the amount. California's Division 9.5 of the Financial Code requires a different list. Section 22802(b) names six items: the total amount of funds provided; the total dollar cost of the financing; the term or estimated term; the method, frequency and amount of payments; a description of prepayment policies; and the total cost of the financing expressed as an annualized rate. Section 22802(a) adds a step that Virginia places in its own section: the provider must obtain the recipient's signature on the disclosure before consummating the transaction. Two jurisdictions, two lists, different counts. That is the fact the lesson turns on: there is no national disclosure document, so a reader who has memorized one list will audit the wrong things in the next state. Which regime governs a particular file is a legal question for counsel, and nothing in this lesson decides it.
lessons.example: Priya audits one offer for a Richmond merchant. The disclosure sheet lists: item 1, $60,000 financing amount, with no separate disbursement figure; item 2, finance charge $21,000; item 3, total repayment $78,300; item 4, estimated 23 payments; item 5, $3,400 weekly by ACH; item 6, draw fee, late payment fee, returned payment fee, no prepayment penalty; item 8, a blanket UCC-1 lien; and no entry for item 9. She reads the statute, counts nine items, and marks each one. Item 7 is conditional by its own words: it is triggered only if the recipient elects to prepay or refinance, so its absence at origination is correct, not a gap. That leaves eight items due at the offer, and her audit returns six present and correct, one present but wrong, and one absent. The wrong one is item 1: the statute requires the disbursement amount if it differs from the financing amount, after any fees deducted or withheld at disbursement, and the sheet quotes only the larger number. The absent one is item 9, the broker-compensation line, which is the item the merchant most wants and the provider's own representative is least likely to volunteer. She then checks the arithmetic the document makes checkable. Item 3 must equal the disbursement amount plus the finance charge: $57,300 + $21,000 = $78,300, which matches, and $57,300 is the disbursement figure item 1 should have carried after the $2,700 fee. She writes both per-dollar measures because they are not the same measure: $78,300 divided by $60,000 is 1.305, and $78,300 divided by the $57,300 the merchant actually receives is 1.3665, which is $136.65 of total repayment per $100 of net proceeds. Her audit line reads: six of eight origination items correct, 75.00 percent, one item present but incomplete, one absent, one conditional item not yet triggered. None of that line is a legal opinion, and all of it is checkable by a second person holding the same two documents.
lessons.question: A disclosure sheet for a Virginia recipient carries items 1 through 6 and item 8, with no item 7 and no item 9. Which reading is correct, and what should the auditor write down?
lessons.answer: Item 7 is conditional and correctly absent, because it is triggered only if the recipient elects to prepay or refinance; item 9 is a required origination item and is missing, so the audit records seven of eight origination items present, with the broker-compensation line outstanding and requested in writing.
lessons.distractor: Both absences are defects: item 7 should show the prepayment policy at origination and item 9 should show the broker fee, so the sheet fails two of nine items and the offer should be treated as non-compliant.
lessons.correction: The statute's item 7 opens with a condition, so its absence at origination is expected; an auditor who reports it missing is auditing from memory rather than from the text. Item 9 has no condition, so its absence is a real gap and the correct response is a written request for the item rather than a conclusion about the offer's validity. Reporting the item count and the condition honestly is the whole skill: one conditional item that has not been triggered, seven of eight origination items present, one outstanding. Whether an omission invalidates anything is a legal question that an advisor does not answer.

depth.definitions: A specific offer is the particular financing offer extended to a particular recipient, as distinct from a rate sheet or a range. A recipient is the person whose principal place of business is in the state and who applies for and is made a specific offer; Virginia adds that a broker cannot be a recipient. A provider extends the specific offer, and a broker obtains or offers to obtain financing for a recipient for compensation or the expectation of it. The disbursement amount is what the recipient receives after fees deducted or withheld at disbursement, and it is the denominator an advisor should use for a per-dollar cost measure. The finance charge is the cost item, and the total repayment amount is defined by the statute as the disbursement amount plus the finance charge, which is what makes the document internally checkable. A conditional item is one whose duty arises only on an event, such as item 7's prepayment or refinance trigger, and an origination item is one due at the offer. Scope is part of every definition: the chapter's exemptions in section 6.2-2229 cover financial institutions, a provider or broker entering into no more than five sales-based financing transactions with a recipient in a 12-month period, and a single transaction over $500,000, and the reliance rule in section 6.2-2232(A) lets a provider rely on a written representation or the business address in the application when deciding whether a principal place of business is in the Commonwealth.
depth.mechanism: The list is a policy instrument, and its mechanism is to convert a negotiation into a document with checkable slots. Before the list, a merchant learned the cost from the remittance that arrived; after it, the cost is stated at the offer, and the arithmetic that ties item 3 to items 1 and 2 can be verified by a third party. Three mechanisms follow. First, an omission becomes visible as a blank rather than as an inference, which is why counting is more reliable than reading for meaning. Second, a specific item changes what is arguable: naming draw fees, late payment fees, returned payment fees and prepayment penalties in item 6 forces the provider either to disclose a fee or to be silent about a fee it charges. Third, the enforcement mechanism is not a fine but enforceability: Virginia provides that a provision of a sales-based financing agreement that violates the chapter is unenforceable against the recipient, and that no agreement may contain a confession of judgment. Alongside the document there is a gate: a provider or broker must register with the State Corporation Commission, disclose in the application any judgment, memorandum of understanding, cease and desist order or conviction involving a crime, fraud, breach of trust or money laundering, pay a $1,000 initial registration fee and a $500 annual fee by September 15, after which a failure to pay makes the registration expire automatically by operation of law. Registration is a fact about the counterparty; disclosure is a fact about the offer; both are read from the source and neither is a credit judgement.
depth.secondExample: The same merchant's file, read under a different regime, shows how the skill transfers. Under California's six-item list, the auditor finds three items with direct Virginia counterparts: the amount provided, the cost of the financing, and the method, frequency and amount of payments. One California item has no Virginia counterpart at all, the total cost of the financing expressed as an annualized rate, and one is a partial counterpart: California asks for a description of prepayment policies where Virginia asks for a description of prepayment policies plus an updated disclosure of items 1 through 6 as of the day of prepayment or refinance. Two California items are therefore new to the reader who learned only the Virginia list, and five Virginia items have no line in the California list at all: the total repayment amount, the estimated number of payments, other potential fees, collateral or security interests, and broker compensation, while a sixth, item 7, is a partial pair because California asks only for a description of prepayment policies whereas Virginia also requires an updated disclosure of items 1 through 6 as of the day of prepayment or refinance. Counting honestly across the pair gives fifteen item slots, four of which are pairs describing the same underlying requirement, so eleven distinct requirements, of which three are exact counterparts, 27.27 percent of the distinct set. A third model is neither list. Utah makes registration the operative duty: the Department of Financial Institutions publishes that under the Commercial Financing Registration and Disclosure Act it is unlawful to engage in a commercial financing transaction as a provider in Utah or with a Utah resident without registering with the Department and maintaining a valid registration, and that the disclosure provisions apply to transactions consummated on or after January 1, 2023. One state puts the document first, another puts the permission first. The reading method is identical in both: find the gate, find the document, count the items, note which are conditional, check the arithmetic, and name the jurisdiction.
depth.mistake: Two errors dominate. The first is treating the California annualized-rate item as an APR and then converting a factor rate into an annual percentage rate on the merchant's behalf. Those are different constructs: a statutory annualized rate is a defined disclosure term produced under that state's method, while a factor is a multiplier applied to an advance, and this course never converts a factor into an APR or describes one as the other. The second error is auditing from memory: an advisor who has read one state's list reports a conditional item as missing, or misses an item that only the other state requires, and then describes the offer as deficient in a conversation with a merchant who will repeat the claim to the provider. The diagnostic is mechanical. If your audit sheet has fewer rows than the statute has numbered items, you have not read the statute; if a row is marked missing and its statutory text begins with a condition, you have misread the row; and if your per-dollar figure uses the financing amount rather than the disbursement amount, your denominator is the wrong one and every comparison built on it inherits the error.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Take two documents from an archive or from the statutory texts themselves, one Virginia sheet and one California sheet, and produce an audit table with one row per numbered item: the item number, the requirement restated in your own words, the status (present and correct, present but wrong, absent, or conditional and not yet triggered), and one line of evidence. Then compute the item-3 check for the Virginia sheet and, for the same file, both per-dollar figures using the financing amount and the disbursement amount, with the difference stated in dollars. Model response: a nine-row Virginia table and a six-row California table, with the conditional row labelled and left open rather than marked missing, the item-3 identity verified as an equality, and two named per-dollar measures that differ because their denominators differ, reported as 1.305 and 1.3665 against a total repayment of $78,300. Rubric: four points for the row counts matching the statutes; three for the conditional item handled correctly; two for the arithmetic identity; two for naming the jurisdiction in the conclusion; one for stating that compliance questions go to counsel. A sheet that reports a percentage of items present without stating which items were conditional, or that gives one per-dollar figure without naming its denominator, scores below half.
depth.summary: A disclosure is read against its statute, not against an impression of what a fair offer says. The transferable habit is the one this project's own accuracy rule requires of its authors: fetch the current text, count the provisions, and refuse to work from an inherited paraphrase. Applied across jurisdictions, the same habit produces a comparison rather than a verdict: nine items here, six there, three exact counterparts, one conditional trigger, two items that appear in only one list, and a registration gate that exists in some states and not others. What the reader gains is not legal certainty but a document whose internal arithmetic can be checked by a second person and whose omissions are visible as blanks. What the reader must not do is announce a conclusion about validity, convert a disclosure's annualized rate into an APR, or substitute a remembered list for the current one.

readings.title: Code of Virginia, Title 6.2, Chapter 22.1, section 6.2-2231 - Disclosure requirements
readings.note: Read the nine numbered items in order and count them. Note that item 7 is conditional by its own words, that item 3 defines total repayment as the disbursement amount plus the finance charge, and that item 9 covers broker compensation. Section-specific to Virginia; it does not describe any other state's regime.

readings.title: Code of Virginia, Title 6.2, Chapter 22.1, section 6.2-2228 - Definitions
readings.note: Read the definitions of recipient, sales-based financing, broker, provider and specific offer. The definition of sales-based financing is worth reading twice because it extends to a true-up mechanism in which repayment is by fixed payment with a reconciliation process adjusting the payment to a percentage of sales or revenue; that sentence is the hook for the next lesson's clause reading.

readings.title: California Financial Code, Division 9.5, section 22802 - Commercial financing disclosures
readings.note: Read subdivision (a) for the signature requirement before consummating the transaction and subdivision (b) for the six required disclosures, counting them. Note the annualized-rate item and compare it against the Virginia list; the two lists are not translations of one another.

readings.title: Utah Department of Financial Institutions - Commercial Financing
readings.note: Read the department's account of the Commercial Financing Registration and Disclosure Act: registration as a provider in Utah or with a Utah resident is unlawful without a valid registration, disclosure duties sit in a separate section, and the disclosure provisions apply to transactions consummated on or after January 1, 2023. This page is the regulator's summary; the underlying code sections are the operative text.

visual.title: Auditing a disclosure document against its statute, item by item
visual.description: A five-step reading sequence that turns a marketing-shaped document into a countable audit, using the Virginia nine-item list as the worked example.
steps: Step 1, find the jurisdiction: identify the recipient's principal place of business, because the item list belongs to that state and not to the product or the funder.
Step 2, fetch the current list: open the statute's disclosure section and write the numbered items into rows before reading the document, so the document cannot set the standard.
Step 3, mark the conditional rows: label any item whose duty arises on an event, such as the prepayment or refinance trigger in item 7, and leave it open instead of marking it absent.
Step 4, score each origination row as present and correct, present but wrong, or absent, writing one line of evidence per row and recording the count as a fraction of origination items.

Step 5, check the arithmetic and both denominators: verify that the total repayment amount equals the disbursement amount plus the finance charge, then state the cost per dollar of the financing amount and per dollar of the disbursement amount separately, naming each denominator.

lessons.title: Reading the clauses that change the number: prepayment, true-up, forum, arbitration and the guarantee
lessons.explanation: Most contracts for business funding state a total repayment amount that a calculator will confirm, and an advisor who checks only that total will conclude that the clauses do not matter. They do, in four distinct ways. First, a clause changes the amount: a prepayment discount, a prepayment penalty, draw fees, late and returned-payment fees, an appraisal, or an insurance premium all move dollars that never appear in the factor. Second, a clause changes the timing: a true-up or reconciliation clause keeps the scheduled remittance fixed while adjusting it against a percentage of sales or revenue, so the tail of the obligation shortens or lengthens with receipts, and the same total is paid over a different number of weeks. Third, a clause changes who bears the loss and where it is borne: a personal guarantee transfers recovery risk to an individual, a forum clause chooses the courthouse, an arbitration clause chooses the process and allocates its cost. Fourth, a clause changes what happens when the clause itself is unlawful. Virginia writes all of this into a single section. Section 6.2-2234(A) requires that any cause of action arising under a sales-based financing contract be brought in a court in the Commonwealth and makes unenforceable any provision mandating that the action be brought outside it. Subdivision (B) provides that a contract containing an arbitration provision may not require face-to-face arbitration proceedings outside the jurisdiction where the recipient's principal place of business is located, that such a provision is unenforceable if it does, and that the provider pays the arbitrators' expenses or fees and any other expenses or administrative fees of the arbitration. Subdivision (C) prohibits any confession by judgment provision or similar provision, which is the device that let a creditor obtain an uncontested judgment against a merchant. The chapter's remedy is enforceability rather than a fine: section 6.2-2236 provides that if any provision of a sales-based financing agreement violates the chapter, that provision is unenforceable against the recipient. None of this is universal; the same clause is read differently in states that have no such statute, and none of it is advice about a particular contract.
lessons.example: Marco reads a $48,000 advance, factor 1.34, repaid over 24 weekly payments. The arithmetic is plain: $48,000 times 1.34 is $64,320.00 of total repayment, divided by 24 gives $2,680.00 a week. He plans for a payoff at week 10 for a merchant who will receive an insurance settlement. At that point the merchant has paid $26,800.00 and the scheduled remaining balance is $37,520.00, which is 58.33 percent of the total repayment. He finds two clauses in the file. Clause A is silent about prepayment: the payoff is the scheduled remaining balance, $37,520.00, so finishing early saves the merchant weeks and no dollars, and the honest sentence is that the payoff equals the remaining scheduled amount. Clause B prices prepayment: a 3 percent discount on the remaining scheduled balance, which is $37,520.00 times 3 percent, or $1,125.60, giving a payoff of $36,394.40. That saving is 3.00 percent of the remaining balance and 1.75 percent of the total repayment, and Marco writes both percentages because the same dollars look large or small depending on the base. He then computes the cost on the denominator that matters, what the merchant receives: a 5 percent fee of $2,400.00 leaves net proceeds of $45,600.00, and $64,320.00 divided by $45,600.00 is 141.05, that is $141.05 of total repayment per $100 of net proceeds, against a nominal factor of 1.34. On the guarantee page he applies the federal rule that holders of at least a 20 percent ownership interest generally must guarantee an SBA loan: in a four-owner company at 25 percent each, all four are generally guarantors, and in a 45, 25, 20 and 10 percent cap table, three are. Finally he prices the clause that a statute may already answer: two witnesses travelling to a forum 1,150 miles away at $620 airfare, two nights at $185 and $120 of ground transport each, plus six hours of business time at $95, comes to $2,790.00, which is the cost of not noticing the forum and arbitration clauses before signing rather than after.
lessons.question: A merchant asks whether prepaying an advance will save money. The contract states the total repayment amount, allows prepayment, and says nothing further. What is the correct answer and the correct calculation?
lessons.answer: The payoff is the scheduled remaining balance, so prepaying saves time and no dollars; the advisor computes what has already been paid against the total repayment and reports both the remaining balance in dollars and the weeks removed, and does not describe a saving that no clause creates.
lessons.distractor: Prepaying always saves the unearned portion of the cost, so the advisor computes the prorated finance charge over the unused weeks and quotes a payoff well below the scheduled remaining balance.
lessons.correction: A saving exists only if a clause creates one. Silence about prepayment means the contracted amount is still owed; a discount clause, a prepayment penalty, or a true-up mechanism each produce a different payoff, and the advisor's job is to read which one is present rather than to assume the contract behaves like an amortising loan. Where a clause does price prepayment, the arithmetic is explicit: the discount applies to the remaining scheduled balance, as in $37,520.00 times 3 percent, or $1,125.60, and the saving is stated both as 3.00 percent of the remaining balance and as 1.75 percent of the total repayment, because the two percentages are both true and neither is the whole truth.

depth.definitions: A prepayment discount reduces the amount owed on early payoff; a prepayment penalty increases it; a clause that is silent on prepayment does neither, and the scheduled balance remains payable. A true-up or reconciliation mechanism keeps a fixed remittance in place while adjusting it against a percentage of sales or revenue: Virginia's definition of sales-based financing expressly includes a financing repaid by a fixed payment that provides for a reconciliation process adjusting the payment to a percentage of sales or revenue, which is why the number of weeks in the tail is an output rather than an input. A forum clause selects where a dispute is heard; an arbitration provision selects the process instead of a court and allocates its costs; a confession of judgment provision lets a creditor obtain a judgment without a contested proceeding, and Virginia prohibits it. A personal guarantee is a promise by an individual, and under the SBA rule holders of at least a 20 percent ownership interest generally must guarantee, while the SBA or the SBA Lender may require other individuals or entities to give full or limited guarantees regardless of ownership percentage when credit or other reasons make it necessary. Insurance and appraisal conditions are cost clauses: hazard insurance is required for 7(a) loans greater than $500,000 and for 504 projects greater than $500,000, and appraisals, surveys or feasibility studies may be required. Each definition belongs to a jurisdiction or a program; the chapter applies in Virginia, and the guarantee rule travels with the SBA guarantee.
depth.mechanism: Clauses change outcomes through four separate channels, and separating them is what keeps a reading from collapsing into a total. The amount channel is familiar: fees, discounts, premiums and penalties are dollars. The timing channel is less familiar and more consequential to a merchant's working capital, because a reconciliation clause ties the completion date to receipts, so a slow quarter extends the obligation while the weekly remittance stays the same; the merchant's cost of the extension is the working capital it removes from operations, not a new fee. The responsibility channel moves the loss: a guarantee does not change the price and changes who pays if the business cannot, which is why the honest conversation names whose assets are exposed rather than treating the guarantee as paperwork. The enforceability channel is the one advisors most often miss: where a statute makes a provision unenforceable, the clause's practical effect is not to bind the merchant but to deter a challenge, so a reader who notices it early anticipates it rather than discovering it under pressure. Running through all four is the asymmetry of information: the provider's representative reads these clauses weekly and the merchant reads them once, so the advisor's value is not legal analysis but translation into dollars, dates and named parties.
depth.secondExample: The same file read on the SBA side shows the same method applied to program conditions rather than to a negotiated contract. The insurance condition is read with its threshold attached: a $520,000 7(a) loan meets the greater-than-$500,000 condition, a 504 project above $500,000 does too, and a $400,000 loan does not, so the reader states the number instead of repeating the clause as a habit. The guarantee rule is read as a two-limb structure: the 20 percent ownership limb is a floor, and the SBA or the SBA Lender may add other guarantors without regard to ownership percentage when credit or other reasons require it, so a cap table with four 25 percent owners does not settle who signs. Appraisals, surveys and feasibility studies are conditions that may be required, which means the reader budgets for them as contingent rather than certain. On the state side, the contrast is direct: Virginia does not price any of this, it removes the clauses it disfavours by making them unenforceable and by prohibiting confession of judgment outright. Two files, two mechanisms, one reading method: find the clause, state its condition, price its effect, and name the authority that governs it.
depth.mistake: The dominant error is the assumption that prepayment is always cheaper, inherited from consumer amortising loans where interest accrues over time. In a purchase of receivables or an advance repaid by a factor, the contracted total is a price rather than accruing interest, so silence about prepayment means the scheduled balance is still owed and the merchant's early finish buys time alone. A second error is treating a statutory prohibition as a guarantee of a good outcome: a clause that Virginia makes unenforceable still costs money to resist, so an advisor who reads it and says nothing leaves the merchant to discover it after a dispute has begun. A third is reading the guarantee as a formality; the SBA rule's ownership threshold and its open second limb mean the question is which individuals are exposed, not whether anyone is. The diagnostic for all three is one sentence an advisor should be able to say about any contract: here is the payoff if we finish early under this clause, here is the clause that decides where a dispute is heard, here is who signs personally, and here is the authority I am reading.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Take one contract or one published template and extract its prepayment, true-up, forum, arbitration, guarantee and insurance provisions into a table with four columns: what the clause says, what it changes (amount, timing, responsibility or enforceability), the dollar or date effect under a stated scenario, and the authority that governs it. Model response: for the $48,000 file the table shows a silent prepayment clause producing a payoff of the remaining scheduled balance of $37,520.00 at week 10 with no dollar saving, a priced variant producing a $1,125.60 discount and a payoff of $36,394.40, a true-up clause that converts the 24-week tail into a range, a forum and arbitration pair read against the state provision requiring in-state actions and prohibiting forced out-of-state face-to-face arbitration, a guarantee line identifying three signers from a 45, 25, 20 and 10 percent cap table, and an insurance line stated with its threshold. Rubric: three points for separating the four channels; three for naming a denominator for every percentage; two for stating each governing authority with its scope; two for naming a cost where a clause creates one; two for writing no conclusion about the merchant's legal position. An answer that asserts a prepayment saving with no clause to support it, or that reports one percentage without its base, cannot pass.
depth.summary: Clauses are read for their effects, not for their presence. The transferable skill is to sort every provision into amount, timing, responsibility or enforceability, then to price it under a stated scenario with a named denominator and a named authority. A total repayment amount confirmed by a calculator is the beginning of the reading, not the end of it: the same $64,320.00 can be owed over 24 weeks, over an unknown number of weeks under a true-up, with or without a $1,125.60 discount, and with three or four individuals personally exposed. Where a state removes a clause by making it unenforceable, the advisor's contribution is early notice and a dollar figure for the cost of contesting, not a legal opinion about who would win.

readings.title: Code of Virginia, section 6.2-2234 - Place for bringing action; certain fees paid by provider; confessions of judgment prohibited
readings.note: Read all three subdivisions: (A) actions must be brought in a court in the Commonwealth and out-of-state forum clauses are unenforceable, (B) arbitration may not require face-to-face proceedings outside the jurisdiction of the recipient's principal place of business and the provider pays the arbitrators' expenses and fees, (C) no confession of judgment provision may appear. Virginia-specific.

readings.title: Code of Virginia, section 6.2-2236 - Validity of noncompliant sales-based financing
readings.note: One sentence, and the most operationally important in the chapter for an advisor reading clauses: a provision of a sales-based financing agreement that violates the chapter is unenforceable against the recipient. Read it after 6.2-2234 so the remedy has something to attach to.

Then read (b) and (c) for appraisals and the hazard-insurance thresholds at $500,000. This section belongs to SBA business loans and does not govern a private advance. The eCFR address redirects to the canonical subpart URL, which resolves normally.

readings.note: Read the section and count its sentences; the current text has five. The third states the commercial credit analysis standard and the fourth permits Lenders, CDCs and SBA to use a business credit scoring model. Useful here because the guarantee and insurance conditions in 120.160 sit on top of this standard rather than replacing it. The address redirects to the canonical subpart URL.

visual.title: Sorting contract clauses into the four channels that change an outcome
visual.description: A labelled decision sequence for reading any funding contract clause and stating its effect in dollars, dates or responsibility rather than in adjectives.
steps: Step 1, read the clause and classify it: does it change the amount owed, the timing of the obligation, who bears the loss, or what happens if the clause itself is unlawful?
Step 2, price the amount channel: apply the actual language to the remaining scheduled balance or the total repayment, and write the result in dollars with the date it applies.

Step 3, map the timing channel: if a true-up or reconciliation is present, state the tail as a range and name what shortens or lengthens it, because the weekly remittance no longer settles the completion date.
Step 4, name the responsibility channel: list every individual a guarantee reaches, using the ownership threshold as a floor and the open second limb as a question, never as a formality.

Step 5, check the enforceability channel against the governing authority, then state the cost of not raising it: a prohibited forum, arbitration or confession-of-judgment provision is a reason for early notice, not a prediction about a dispute.

lessons.title: Reading the public record: what a UCC-1 filing, a continuation and a bankruptcy stay do and do not prove
lessons.explanation: The public record is a set of filings, not a narrative, and reading it means reading three documents as they actually function in law. The first is the financing statement under Article 9 of the Uniform Commercial Code. Section 9-502(a) provides that a financing statement is sufficient only if it gives the name of the debtor, the name of the secured party or a representative of the secured party, and an indication of the collateral covered. Three elements, and sufficiency requires no more. Section 9-504 then provides that a financing statement sufficiently indicates the collateral if it describes the collateral under section 9-108 or if it simply indicates that the statement covers all assets or all personal property. A single sentence on a one-page filing can therefore reach everything the debtor owns, which is why the number of filings in a search result tells a reader much less than the collateral line on each one. Section 9-515 sets the clock. Subsection (a) makes a filed financing statement effective for five years after the date of filing; subsection (c) provides that effectiveness lapses on the expiration of that period unless a continuation statement is filed before the lapse, that on lapse the statement ceases to be effective and any security interest perfected by it becomes unperfected unless it is perfected otherwise, and that when it becomes unperfected on lapse it is deemed never to have been perfected as against a purchaser of the collateral for value; subsection (d) allows a continuation statement to be filed only within the six months before the expiration of the five-year period; and subsection (e) continues effectiveness for five years commencing on the day the statement would have become ineffective. The second document is the bankruptcy petition, and the relevant rule is statutory rather than contractual. 11 U.S.C. section 362(a) provides that a petition operates as a stay, applicable to all entities, of eight enumerated categories of action, including the commencement or continuation of a proceeding against the debtor to recover a claim that arose before the case, the enforcement of a judgment obtained before the case, any act to obtain possession of property of the estate, any act to create, perfect or enforce a lien against property of the estate, and any act to collect, assess or recover a pre-petition claim; subsection (b) lists the categories to which the stay does not apply. The third document is the one that does not exist: nothing in the record states whether the debtor can pay, what the collateral is worth, or whether a release will be given on payoff. A state filing office says the same thing in one line: a financing statement is filed to perfect a security interest in named collateral and establishes priority in case of debtor default or bankruptcy. Priority, not solvency.
lessons.example: A search run on 2026-10-01 for a merchant file returns three filings. The first was filed 2019-08-02 and covers all assets. The second was filed 2026-03-15 and covers two specific pieces of equipment. The third was filed 2024-05-11 by a second funder. Reading the dates instead of the names produces the analysis. The 2019-08-02 statement had five years of effectiveness, which expired on 2024-08-02, and a continuation statement could have been filed only within the six months before that date, that is from 2024-02-02 to 2024-08-02. The search shows no continuation, so on the statute's terms that security interest became unperfected on lapse unless it is perfected otherwise, and as against a purchaser of the collateral for value it is deemed never to have been perfected at all. That is a different conclusion from the one a reader reaches by seeing a blanket lien and assuming it binds everything. The 2026-03-15 equipment filing is effective for five years, to 2031-03-15, which is 1,826 days, and its continuation window opens on 2030-09-15, so it is a dated obligation rather than a permanent condition. The third filing is read the same way, by date and collateral line, and nothing in it states an amount owed or whether it was repaid. The cost of this reading is small: three searches at $22.00 each is $66.00, plus 1.5 hours at $95.00, which is $142.50, so $208.50 to know the position before a file is submitted instead of afterwards. One week later the merchant's business files a bankruptcy petition. Because the stay under 11 U.S.C. section 362(a) operates on all entities and reaches any act to collect, assess or recover a claim that arose before the case, a debit scheduled for the next business day is a collection act, and the funder's contractual right to debit does not suspend a statute. The advisor's note therefore separates two lists. What the record proves: three filings with three dates, one apparently lapsed, one blanket and two specific, and one petition. What the record does not prove: whether the merchant can pay, whether the collateral would realise its book value, whether a payoff letter will be honoured, or what a court would say about any of it.
lessons.question: A UCC search shows a blanket financing statement filed 2019-08-02 with no continuation statement, and the merchant's advisor says the business is unencumbered. What is wrong with that sentence?
lessons.answer: The filing had five years of effectiveness expiring 2024-08-02 and a continuation could only be filed in the six months before that date; with no continuation the security interest became unperfected on lapse and is deemed never perfected as against a purchaser for value, which is a statement about UCC priority and not a statement that the business is unencumbered or that no obligation remains.
lessons.distractor: The filing still binds the business because financing statements run indefinitely until a termination statement is filed, so the search result means the merchant is encumbered and any new funder would take a junior position.
lessons.correction: Effectiveness is time-limited: five years from filing, with a continuation statement permitted only in the six months before expiration and continuing effectiveness for five years from the date the statement would have lapsed. A lapse unperfecteds the security interest and, as against a purchaser for value, unwinds it retroactively, which is why a reader must date every filing rather than count them. The obligation itself is a separate question the record does not answer; a debt can survive the lapse of perfection, and a filing that has lapsed says nothing about whether money is still owed or whether a release would be given. Saying the business is unencumbered overstates what the search proves, and saying it is encumbered overstates what the filing still does.

depth.definitions: A financing statement is the public filing that perfects a security interest; a secured party is the creditor of record; the debtor is the named person; an indication of collateral is the line that describes what the filing reaches, and it may be as broad as all assets or all personal property. Perfection is the legal step that makes a security interest effective against third parties, and priority is the ranking between competing interests. A lapse is the expiry of a financing statement's effectiveness, and a continuation statement is the filing that prevents it, permitted only inside a six-month window. A purchaser for value is the party against whom a lapsed and thus unwound perfection is measured. The automatic stay is the statutory bar on the eight categories of action listed in 11 U.S.C. section 362(a); property of the estate is the debtor's property that the estate comprises; a pre-petition claim is one arising before the case commenced. Two scope notes belong here: the Article 9 text used in these lessons is the uniform text as published, while each state enacts its own version and its own filing office rules, and a state filing is read at the filing office rather than from a summary. Neither the statute nor a search result is evidence of the amount owed.
depth.mechanism: Three mechanisms explain why the record reads the way it does. The first is minimal sufficiency: because section 9-502(a) requires only three elements and section 9-504 permits an all-assets indication, a filing that looks casual can reach everything, and a filing that looks comprehensive can reach nothing relevant if the debtor's name is wrong. The second is the maintenance clock, which converts a filing into a recurring obligation rather than a permanent condition. Five years of effectiveness, a six-month continuation window, and a lapse that unwinds perfection as against a purchaser for value together mean that the operational question is not whether a lien exists but whether it is still effective on the date that matters. The third is that the bankruptcy stay operates on conduct rather than on intent or contract: it binds all entities and reaches collection acts, so a debit, a demand letter or a setoff executed after a petition is a stay violation regardless of what the contract says. The stay delays enforcement rather than extinguishing a claim, which is why a file can be simultaneously uncollectible this week and solvent on paper. These mechanisms are why the search, the payoff letter and the legal question are three separate work products, and why an advisor states one and stops.
depth.secondExample: The same record read for a different reader produces a different work product, and the contrast is the point. A second-position funder reads the search to decide whether to fund: it wants the collateral line and the date on every filing, the payoff amount for each recorded interest, and a decision about whether the blanket filing, if effective, leaves anything to take; its conclusion is a position, and it may still fund. The merchant's advisor reads the same record to produce a document the merchant can act on: a plain list of who has filed against the business, on what date, against what collateral, whether that filing is still effective under the five-year clock, who holds a release, and which items require the merchant's own signature to clear. The third contrast is the filing office itself. California's Secretary of State publishes that a financing statement on Form UCC1 is filed to perfect a security interest in named collateral and to establish priority in case of default or bankruptcy, that the form must be reproduced in the format prescribed by the Uniform Commercial Code and that submittals not conforming are rejected, and that UCC filings are public records, with an explicit warning not to include Social Security numbers or other nonessential personal information. That warning matters to an advisor handling merchant documents: the record is public, so a file the advisor assembles should not create exposure the merchant did not have.
depth.mistake: Three misreadings recur. The first is treating a clean search as a clean file: a search answers a question about recorded interests at a moment, so the honest sentence always carries the date and the debtor name searched. The second is treating a filing as proof of debt. A financing statement proves that a secured party filed, not that a balance is owed, not that it was never repaid, and not that a release will be refused; the amount question is answered by a payoff letter with a date and an expiry. The third is treating a bankruptcy petition as the end of the obligation or as an occasion to act quickly. The stay binds all entities and reaches collection acts, so a funder's scheduled debit after a petition is the violation the statute names, and a merchant's advisor who tells the merchant to move money is describing conduct rather than a legal position. The diagnostic is a single test: read your own note back and mark every sentence that includes a date, a collateral line or a statutory citation. If a conclusion about the record has none of the three, it is an impression rather than a reading.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Given a search result with at least three filings, produce a one-page record read with four lines per filing: date filed, collateral as indicated, date of effectiveness expiry, and the continuation window open and close dates; then add one column titled what this filing does not prove, and one closing paragraph titled what I would need before relying on this record. Model response: for the worked file, the 2019-08-02 all-assets filing expires 2024-08-02 with a continuation window of 2024-02-02 to 2024-08-02 and no continuation shown, so it is described as lapsed and unwound as against a purchaser for value, while the obligation itself is listed as unverified; the 2026-03-15 equipment filing runs to 2031-03-15, 1,826 days, with a window opening 2030-09-15; the 2024-05-11 filing is recorded with its own dates; and the closing paragraph lists a payoff letter per recorded interest, a certified search in the correct debtor name, and counsel's view on the lapse question. Rubric: three points for dating every filing correctly; three for stating the collateral indication in the filing's own words; two for separating lapsed perfection from an outstanding obligation; two for the record-does-not-prove column; two for the closing paragraph naming what would change the reading. A response that reports only names and totals, or that concludes the business is unencumbered, scores below half.
depth.summary: Public filings answer narrow questions precisely and broad questions not at all. The transferable skill is to read each filing with three facts attached, its date, its collateral indication and its effectiveness under the five-year clock, and then to state separately what the record leaves open: the amount owed, the value of the collateral, the willingness to release, and the effect of a bankruptcy petition that stays collection acts by statute rather than by agreement. What makes this lesson different from the earlier file-reading lessons is its object: not the merchant's conduct, but the instruments other creditors have already filed, which is the part of a file that no conversation with the merchant can supply.

readings.title: Uniform Commercial Code, section 9-502 - Contents of financing statement
readings.note: Read subsection (a) and count the three sufficiency elements: debtor name, secured party name, indication of the collateral. The lesson cites this as the uniform text; states enact their own versions, and the filing office's rules govern the form. Subsection (b) concerns real-property-related filings and can be skimmed.

readings.title: Uniform Commercial Code, section 9-515 - Duration and effectiveness of financing statement; effect of lapsed financing statement
readings.note: Read (a) for the five-year period, (c) for lapse and the retroactive effect against a purchaser for value, (d) for the six-month continuation window, and (e) for the continuation of effectiveness for five years from the date the statement would have lapsed. This is the section that makes every search result a question about dates.

readings.title: 11 U.S. Code section 362 - Automatic stay
readings.note: Read subsection (a) and count the eight enumerated categories, with attention to the collection, lien-enforcement, possession and judgment-enforcement items; then read the opening of subsection (b) to see that the stay is not universal. The statute is long, so read (a) and the first few exceptions rather than the whole section.

readings.title: California Secretary of State - UCC Financing Statement (Form UCC1)
readings.note: A filing office's own one-paragraph account of what a financing statement does: filed to perfect a security interest in named collateral and to establish priority in case of debtor default or bankruptcy. Note also its statement that the form must be reproduced in the prescribed format and its warning that UCC filings are public records, so advisors should not file unnecessary personal information.

visual.title: Reading a UCC search result as dates, collateral and open questions
visual.description: A labelled sequence that converts a list of filings into a position statement with explicit gaps, using the three-filing worked file.
steps: Step 1, anchor the search: record the date the search was run and the exact debtor name searched, because every conclusion is provisional on both.
Step 2, date each filing: for every entry, add five years to the filing date to get the effectiveness expiry, then mark the six-month continuation window that precedes it.

Step 3, read each collateral indication in the filing's own words, noting whether it is a description under section 9-108 or an all-assets indication under section 9-504, because one line can reach everything.

Step 4, mark lapses explicitly: a filing with no continuation inside its window is described as lapsed and unwound as against a purchaser for value, with the obligation itself left listed as unverified.
Step 5, split the page into proved and not proved, and treat a later bankruptcy petition as a statutory bar on collection acts by all entities rather than as a reason to move faster.

lessons.title: Reading tax-basis statements: cash versus accrual, constructive receipt and the reconciling footnote
lessons.explanation: A tax return is prepared for a different purpose than a funding decision, and the way to read one is to establish the accounting method it uses and then rebuild the cash. The instructions to Schedule C say that generally a taxpayer can use the cash method, an accrual method, or any other method permitted by the Internal Revenue Code, and that in all cases the method used must clearly reflect income. Under the cash method, the return shows all items of taxable income actually or constructively received during the year, and income is constructively received when it is credited to the taxpayer's account or made available without restriction; it shows amounts actually paid for deductible expenses, with the caveat that a payment creating an asset with a useful life extending beyond twelve months, or beyond the end of the next tax year, may not be deductible in the year of payment or may be only partly deductible. Publication 538 sets out the family of methods, the rule that if an inventory is necessary to account for income an accrual method must be used for purchases and sales subject to the small business exception, the rule that a taxpayer who uses the cash method for income must use the cash method for expenses, the all-events test for accrual income, and for taxpayers with an applicable financial statement an income-inclusion rule requiring the amount to be reported at the earliest of the five events the publication lists: payment received, the amount due, the income earned, title passing, or inclusion as revenue in the applicable financial statement. Two further facts change how a return reads. First, a cash-basis return and a bank statement legitimately differ, and the reader's obligation is to reconcile them rather than to suspect one of them. Second, a change of method carries a transition: the Schedule C instructions state that changing the accounting method generally requires Form 3115, that a net negative section 481(a) adjustment is generally taken into account in the year of change, that a net positive section 481(a) adjustment is generally taken into account over four years, and that a net positive adjustment is reported on line 6. An advisor who compares a return with deposits without knowing the method, the timing rules and any section 481(a) item will misread the business in both directions, overstating it when receipts are accrued and collected late, and understating it when the return carries an adjustment that belongs to an earlier year.
lessons.example: The Braxton file shows all three readings at once. Schedule C for the most recent year shows gross receipts of $412,000 and net profit of $96,400 on line 31, and line F records the cash method. Bank deposits for the same period total $468,000. The $56,000 gap resolves into three items: $40,000 of loan proceeds, which are not income; $9,500 of an owner contribution, which is not income; and $6,500 of a returned supplier deposit, which is not income. $412,000 plus $40,000 plus $9,500 plus $6,500 equals $468,000, which is an exact reconciliation, and the advisor writes it as an equality rather than describing a discrepancy. In the other direction, $58,000 of December invoices were collected in January, so they are missing from this cash-basis return entirely: that is 14.08 percent of reported cash receipts, and the same business reporting on the accrual method would show receipts of $470,000. The number the advisor actually needs is neither of those. Net profit is not cash available to service a new remittance, and three adjustments make the difference: add back depreciation of $14,800, which is a deduction and not a cash outflow; subtract principal payments on existing debt of $62,400, which are cash and not an expense; and subtract owner draws of $48,000, which are cash and not an expense. $96,400 plus $14,800 minus $62,400 minus $48,000 equals $800.00. One file says the business earned $96,400 and the same file says $800.00 of free cash remains after the two adjustments a return does not make for you; an advisor who quotes only the first number has not read the document. Finally there is the footnote. The merchant's accountant filed Form 3115 and reported a net positive section 481(a) adjustment of $24,000, which is generally taken into account over four years, so $6,000.00 a year, or $500.00 a month, will appear in future taxable income that has nothing to do with future trading. The advisor records it as a timing item, not as profit and not as a problem.
lessons.question: A merchant supplies a cash-basis return showing $96,400 of net profit and bank statements showing $468,000 of deposits, and asks how much the business can afford in new weekly payments. What must the advisor do before answering?
lessons.answer: Reconcile the two figures item by item so that every dollar of the $56,000 difference is classified as non-income or income, then rebuild cash by adjusting net profit for non-cash deductions, cash payments that are not expenses and owner draws, and state the resulting figure with its assumptions, because net profit is not cash available and deposits are not revenue.
lessons.distractor: Average the two figures, since the deposits include some non-income items and the return omits some collected receipts, and use the midpoint as a conservative estimate of the cash available for a new remittance.
lessons.correction: Averaging two measures that answer different questions produces a number that answers neither. The reconciliation is exact and checkable: $412,000 of receipts plus $40,000 of loan proceeds plus $9,500 of owner contribution plus $6,500 of returned deposit equals $468,000 of deposits. The cash rebuild is equally explicit: $96,400 plus $14,800 of depreciation minus $62,400 of principal payments minus $48,000 of owner draws equals $800.00. The advisor's answer is that figure with those four components named, plus the $58,000 of December receivables collected in January as a timing fact and the $6,000.00 annual section 481(a) item as a separate one. Nothing in the answer promises what a funder will do with any of it.

depth.definitions: Under the cash method, income is reported when actually or constructively received and expenses when actually paid; constructive receipt means the income is credited to the taxpayer's account or made available without restriction. Under an accrual method, income is reported when the all-events test is met, which the publication describes as all events having occurred that fix the right to receive the income with the amount determinable with reasonable accuracy, and expenses follow economic performance rather than payment. A hybrid method combines elements, subject to the restrictions that an inventory-based business must use an accrual method for purchases and sales unless the small business exception applies, and that a taxpayer using cash for income must use cash for expenses. Schedule C line F is where the method is declared, and line 31 is net profit or loss, which is the tax figure and not a cash figure. A section 481(a) adjustment is the transition amount required to prevent income or expense from being duplicated or omitted when a method changes; the instructions state that a net negative adjustment is generally taken into account in the year of change and a net positive adjustment generally over four years. An applicable financial statement is a defined financial statement that triggers the income-inclusion rule. Scope: Schedule C is filed by sole proprietors, other entities file other returns, and whether a particular item is deductible is a question for the merchant's tax preparer, not for a funding advisor.
depth.mechanism: Net profit differs from cash for three structural reasons, and naming them is what makes a forecast honest. The first is non-cash deductions: depreciation, amortisation and some allowances reduce taxable income without moving money. The second is cash movements that are not expenses: principal repayments on debt, owner draws and distributions, purchases of equipment, and deposits into reserve accounts. The third is the method's own timing rules, which can shift a whole quarter of receipts across a year boundary, as with December invoices collected in January under the cash method, or pull income forward under the accrual all-events test and the applicable-financial-statement inclusion rule. A fourth, less common, mechanism is a transition item such as a section 481(a) adjustment, which inserts an amount that belongs to an earlier period into a later year. The reason the return is still the best single document available is that it is prepared by a third party, signed under penalty of perjury, and constrained by rules that leave a detectable trail; the reason it is not sufficient is that it is annual, so a business with a strong year and a weak final quarter reads identically to one with twelve steady months, and the reader who needs a remittance cadence is asking about months, not years.
depth.secondExample: The same reconstruction on a different set of documents shows which parts of the skill transfer. A corporation that has elected S status files Form 1120-S, and the shareholder-facing figures arrive on Schedules K and K-1, where each shareholder receives a pro rata share of the corporation's items rather than a single net profit number, so the advisor can no longer read one line as the owner's income; the items are reported separately, and ordinary business income on the K-1 is only one of them. A merchandiser adds a second complication: where an inventory is necessary to account for income, an accrual method must be used for purchases and sales unless the small business taxpayer exception applies, so the presence or absence of an inventory method on the return is itself information about how the figures were produced, and a change to treating inventory items as non-incidental materials and supplies is a method change with its own section 481(a) arithmetic. Put the two together and the reading method is unchanged: establish the entity and the method, identify which figures are tax figures, rebuild the cash with named adjustments, and state the timing items separately. What changes is only which documents you ask for and which line is the starting point.
depth.mistake: The first error is reading deposits as revenue. Deposits contain loan proceeds, owner contributions, transfers between accounts and refunds, all of which the return correctly excludes, so a deposit-based revenue estimate can overstate receipts by a wide margin and produce a payment that fits on paper and not in the account. The second error is quoting net profit as available cash: the Braxton rebuild moves $96,400 to $800.00, a difference of $95,600, and a recommendation built on the first figure would exceed the merchant's capacity by a factor of more than a hundred. The third is treating a section 481(a) adjustment as improved or deteriorated performance, when it is an accounting transition that will appear in a future year regardless of trading. The diagnostic is to write the rebuild as an equation with a sign in front of every line and then check whether it starts from receipts, from net profit or from deposits. If the equation does not name which of the three is the starting point and why, the forecast has no base.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Take a return summary and a deposit total for one business and produce a one-page rebuild with three labelled sections: the reconciliation from deposits to reported receipts, in which every difference is classified as income, non-income deposit or timing difference; the cash rebuild from net profit, in which every line is labelled non-cash deduction, cash-not-expense, draw or timing item; and a limitations paragraph naming what the documents cannot show. Model response: receipts of $412,000 plus $40,000 of loan proceeds plus $9,500 of owner contribution plus $6,500 of returned deposit equals $468,000 of deposits, an exact reconciliation; net profit of $96,400 plus $14,800 of depreciation minus $62,400 of principal minus $48,000 of draws equals $800.00 of free cash, with the $58,000 of December receivables and the $6,000.00 annual section 481(a) item listed as timing facts; and the limitations paragraph stating that the return is annual, that the merchant's preparer owns any tax conclusion, and that no funder's decision is predicted. Rubric: three points for the reconciliation balancing to the dollar; three for the cash rebuild with signed lines and correct labels; two for stating the section 481(a) item as timing rather than performance; two for naming the method and the entity type; two for the limitations paragraph. A rebuild that starts from deposits, or that reports net profit as available cash, cannot pass.
depth.summary: Tax documents are read for their basis, not for their headline. The transferable method is four steps in order: establish the entity and the method, reconcile every difference between deposits and reported receipts, rebuild cash from net profit with labelled adjustments, and set timing items apart from trading. Applied consistently it turns a plausible story about a profitable business into a specific statement that a business reporting $96,400 of net profit has, on these documents and before any new obligation, $800.00 of free cash a year after principal payments and draws, plus a known $6,000.00 of transition income that belongs to earlier years. That is a figure a merchant can challenge and an underwriter can check, which is exactly what makes it usable.

readings.title: IRS Instructions for Schedule C (Form 1040), Line F - Accounting method
readings.note: Read the Line F discussion in full: the choice among cash, accrual and other permitted methods and the requirement that the method clearly reflect income; the cash-method treatment of income actually or constructively received and of amounts actually paid; the limit on deducting a payment that creates an asset with a useful life beyond twelve months or the end of the next tax year; and the statements about Form 3115, section 481(a) adjustments and the line where a net positive adjustment is reported. These instructions are for Schedule C filers, so they describe sole proprietors rather than every entity.

readings.title: IRS Publication 538, Accounting Periods and Methods
readings.note: Read the overview of the methods and of the hybrid method with its restrictions on inventory-based businesses and on mixing cash income with accrual expenses; then read the accrual discussion of the all-events test and the applicable-financial-statement income inclusion rule. Long publication; the sections named here are the ones the lesson uses.

readings.title: IRS Instructions for Form 1120-S, Schedules K and K-1 (shareholder's pro rata share items)
readings.note: Read the general instructions on Schedules K and K-1 to see why an S corporation does not present one net profit figure for its owner: items flow to shareholders separately and pro rata. This is what makes the reading method change entity by entity, and it is the document to request instead of a Schedule C when the business is an S corporation.

visual.title: Rebuilding cash from a tax return in three signed steps
visual.description: A labelled sequence that separates a tax figure from a cash figure and makes every intervening item explicit and checkable.
steps: Step 1, establish the basis: record the entity type and the accounting method from the return, because the method decides which receipts appear in this year and which do not.

Step 2, reconcile deposits to reported receipts and classify every difference as income, non-income deposit or timing difference, writing the reconciliation as an equality that must balance to the dollar.

Step 3, start the cash rebuild from net profit and attach a sign to every adjustment: add non-cash deductions such as depreciation, subtract cash flows that are not expenses such as principal payments and owner draws.
Step 4, pull timing items out of the trading picture, including receipts collected after the year end and any section 481(a) transition amount, and state each as a separate annual or monthly figure.
Step 5, write the limitations paragraph before the recommendation, naming what the annual documents cannot show and who owns any tax conclusion.

lessons.title: Reading a conditional offer: counteroffers, conditions and the gap between a signed term sheet and money
lessons.explanation: An offer letter is not funding, and reading one properly means answering three separate questions. The first is what the offer says in dollars. The second is what it conditions, because conditions that are absent from the letter are not absent from the transaction. The third is what the law says about the distance between what the merchant requested and what came back, and here the text is unusually clear. Under Regulation B, adverse action includes a refusal to grant credit in substantially the amount or on substantially the terms requested in an application, unless the creditor makes a counteroffer to grant credit in a different amount or on other terms and the applicant uses or expressly accepts the credit offered. The carve-out is explicit, and it decides what happens next: a counteroffer the merchant expressly accepts is not a refusal in substantially the amount or terms requested, while a refusal in substantially the amount and terms requested is adverse action, and the notification provisions of the regulation then govern what the applicant is told and when, subject to the business-credit rules that depend on the applicant's gross revenues. Whether those provisions reach a particular non-bank funder and a particular merchant is a legal question, not an advisor's conclusion. On the terms themselves, the SBA's lending criteria section is worth reading in full and counting, because its structure is frequently misreported from memory. The current text has five sentences: the applicant, including an Operating Company, must be creditworthy; loans must be so sound as to reasonably assure repayment; Lenders and CDCs must use appropriate and prudent generally acceptable commercial credit analysis processes and procedures consistent with those used for their similarly sized, non-SBA guaranteed commercial loans; Lenders, CDCs and SBA may use a business credit scoring model; and, when approving direct or guaranteed loans, they may consider as applicable the credit score or credit history of the applicant and the Operating Company if applicable, its Associates and any guarantors, the earnings or cashflow of the applicant, or where applicable any equity or collateral. The fourth sentence is the one that a paraphrase from an older version of the section tends to drop, and it matters for how a file is described: a business credit scoring model may be used, which is not the same as saying that a score approves a loan. The conditions live in their own section, which states what is normally required for SBA business loans: guarantees by holders of at least 20 percent ownership interests, appraisals, surveys or feasibility studies as SBA may require, and hazard insurance above stated thresholds. A term sheet that does not mention them is not a term sheet without conditions; it is a term sheet whose conditions arrive later.
lessons.example: Alder Supply applies for $85,000 repaid over 24 weekly payments at a factor of 1.30. Read the request: total repayment is $85,000 times 1.30, or $110,500.00; the weekly remittance is $110,500.00 divided by 24, or $4,604.17; a 3 percent fee of $2,550.00 leaves net proceeds of $82,450.00; and $110,500.00 divided by $82,450.00 is $134.02 of total repayment per $100 of net proceeds. The funder returns a counteroffer: $60,000 over 20 weekly payments at 1.38. Read it the same way: total repayment $82,800.00; weekly $4,140.00; a 3 percent fee of $1,800.00 leaves net proceeds of $58,200.00; and $82,800.00 divided by $58,200.00 is $142.27 per $100 of net proceeds. Three comparisons belong in the note, because they point in different directions: the amount is 29.41 percent smaller, the duration is 16.67 percent shorter, and the cost per dollar of net proceeds is 6.16 percent higher. Weekly, the merchant remits $464.17 less than under the request, which is why the counteroffer feels easier, and at a contribution of $12,400 a week it consumes 33.39 percent of that contribution against 37.13 percent for the request. The merchant expressly accepts the counteroffer, and that single fact settles the regulatory reading: an accepted counteroffer is not a refusal in substantially the amount or terms requested, so the file does not become an adverse action on these facts. Had the merchant refused it, the refusal would be adverse action, and the notification question would follow with its own timing rules. Two conditions remain open in the file regardless of which way that reading goes: there is no payoff letter for an existing obligation that debits $3,100 a week, and the funder's condition list has not been produced in writing. The advisor's note therefore ends with three dated lines: the offer as read, the counteroffer as accepted, the current outstanding obligations at $3,100 a week, and the sentence that matters most, that this is an offer with conditions and no money has moved.
lessons.question: A funder responds to an $85,000 request with an offer of $60,000 at a higher factor, and the merchant accepts it in writing the same day. What is the correct description of this file, and what has to happen next?
lessons.answer: It is an accepted counteroffer, which the regulation expressly excludes from adverse action, so no adverse action notification is triggered by the response itself; what happens next is a written condition list, a payoff letter for every existing obligation, and confirmation of the terms as accepted, because the offer is not funding.
lessons.distractor: It is a decline on the request, so an adverse action notice with the reasons must be sent, and the merchant should request the reasons in writing to preserve the notification timeline.
lessons.correction: The regulation's definition turns on whether the applicant uses or expressly accepts the credit offered: an accepted counteroffer is not a refusal in substantially the amount or on substantially the terms requested, and calling it a decline misdescribes the file and invites a notice that the definition does not require. If instead the merchant refuses the counteroffer, the refusal is adverse action and the notification provisions apply, with the business-credit rules that depend on the applicant's gross revenues. In both cases the advisor's next work product is the same: a dated list of open conditions, including a payoff letter for the existing $3,100 weekly obligation, and a statement that no funds have been disbursed.

depth.definitions: A term sheet or offer letter states proposed terms; a commitment letter is a stronger instrument and its strength is a contract question; a conditional approval is an approval subject to named conditions; a counteroffer is a new proposal in a different amount or on different terms. Adverse action is defined by regulation to include a refusal to grant credit in substantially the amount or on substantially the terms requested, unless the creditor makes a counteroffer and the applicant uses or expressly accepts the credit offered, and also includes a termination of an account or an unfavourable change in its terms that does not affect a class of accounts, and a refusal to increase credit on request. Creditworthy and reasonably assured repayment are the standards stated in the SBA's lending criteria section, alongside the requirement that Lenders and CDCs use appropriate and prudent generally acceptable commercial credit analysis processes and procedures consistent with those used for similarly sized non-SBA guaranteed commercial loans. A business credit scoring model is a permitted input under the fourth sentence of that section. Conditions in SBA lending sit in a separate section and cover guarantees by holders of at least 20 percent of ownership, appraisals, surveys or feasibility studies, and hazard insurance above thresholds. Scope notes: the regulation's application to a given business credit applicant is a legal question, and the SBA sections bind SBA business loans rather than private transactions.
depth.mechanism: Three mechanisms explain why conditional offers are so often misread. The first is that a counteroffer changes economics and psychology in opposite directions: fewer dollars and a shorter tail make the payment easier to carry, while a higher factor and a fee on a smaller base raise the cost per dollar of net proceeds, so the merchant's relief and the merchant's cost move together. Reading them together is the entire value of the comparison. The second is the sequencing of conditions: funders state price first and conditions at underwriting or close, so a letter that reads like a decision is a preliminary statement, and the reader who dates every condition and writes them into a list is the one who is not surprised. The third is the legal structure of the response itself: the regulation makes the difference between a refusal and an accepted counteroffer decide whether a notification duty exists, which means the same set of numbers can be either an adverse action or not depending on one sentence of the merchant's reply. That is why the advisor records the merchant's acceptance or refusal with a date, and why an offer is described as an offer until funds are disbursed. Under all three runs the credit-scoring sentence: a model may be used, a score is an input, and neither the section nor the model promises an outcome.
depth.secondExample: The same method applied to an SBA-guaranteed file shows how conditions behave when they are stated in advance. A lender issues an approval subject to several conditions: guarantees from each holder of at least 20 percent of the ownership interest, with the possibility that other individuals or entities may be required to give full or limited guarantees without regard to ownership percentage when credit or other reasons make it necessary; an appraisal or feasibility study if SBA requires one; and hazard insurance if the loan exceeds the $500,000 threshold. The program context is stated with its numbers rather than as a general claim: 7(a) loans run up to $5 million with maturity of 10 years or less unless the financing is for real estate or equipment with a useful life exceeding 10 years, and 25 years including extensions for real estate; CDC/504 projects run from $25,000 to $5.5 million; and microloans are up to $50,000. The contrast with a private counteroffer is that in the SBA file the conditions are published before the offer, so the reader's job is to check them off, while in a private file the reader must demand the list in writing. In both, eligibility and approval are decisions made by the funder or by SBA and not by the advisor, and the advisor's sentences stay in the conditional: if these conditions clear, then the terms are as stated.
depth.mistake: The first error is equating an approval with money, which is how merchants commit to equipment orders, hires or leases on the strength of a conditional letter and then discover what a condition is. The second is describing the SBA lending criteria from an inherited paraphrase: the current section has five sentences, and the fourth permits Lenders, CDCs and SBA to use a business credit scoring model. An advisor who repeats the older four-sentence summary has dropped the sentence that speaks directly to how modern decisions are made, and a reviewer who checks the section will find the error immediately. The third is treating a counteroffer as a decline without asking whether the merchant accepted it, which produces the wrong regulatory description and, in some files, a notice that was never required.
