The diagnostic is to write two sentences and check them against the text: how many sentences does the lending criteria section have, and does the definition of adverse action carve out an accepted counteroffer? If either answer comes from memory, the file is being read from a paraphrase.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Given one request and one counteroffer, produce a one-page read with four rows (amount, duration, total repayment and cost per $100 of net proceeds, weekly remittance as a percentage of contribution), a dated open-conditions list, and one sentence describing the file's regulatory status on the facts. Model response: request $85,000 over 24 weeks at 1.30, total repayment $110,500.00, weekly $4,604.17, $134.02 per $100 of net proceeds, 37.13 percent of a $12,400 weekly contribution; counteroffer $60,000 over 20 weeks at 1.38, total repayment $82,800.00, weekly $4,140.00, $142.27 per $100 of net proceeds, 33.39 percent of contribution; 29.41 percent less amount, 16.67 percent shorter, 6.16 percent more expensive per dollar; conditions outstanding: payoff letter for the $3,100 weekly obligation, written condition list, confirmation of accepted terms; regulatory sentence: the merchant expressly accepted the counteroffer, which the adverse action definition carves out, and no funds have been disbursed. Rubric: three points for the four comparisons with correct arithmetic; two for naming the denominators; two for the dated conditions list; two for the regulatory sentence grounded in the definition rather than in impression; one for stating that approval is not the advisor's to give. A response that calls an accepted counteroffer a decline, or that reports the offer as funding, scores below half.
depth.summary: A conditional offer is read as a set of proposed terms, a set of undated conditions and a legal event. The transferable habits are three: compare the counteroffer on amount, duration and cost per dollar of net proceeds rather than on the weekly payment alone; require conditions in writing and date each one; and describe the file in the vocabulary of the regulation, where an accepted counteroffer is expressly excluded from adverse action and a refusal in substantially the amount or terms requested is not. Underwriting judgement stays with the funder, and the advisor's contribution is a comparison a merchant can check and a conditions list a merchant can clear.

readings.title: eCFR - 13 CFR 120.150, SBA's lending criteria
readings.note: Read the section and count its sentences, then identify which one permits a business credit scoring model. The current text as amended by 88 FR 21085 has five sentences and the fourth is the scoring sentence. Do not rely on a summary carried in older materials. The eCFR address redirects to the canonical subpart URL, which resolves normally.

readings.title: eCFR - 13 CFR 120.160, Loan conditions
readings.note: Read (a) for the guarantee rule and its 20 percent ownership threshold, (b) for appraisals, surveys or feasibility studies, and (c) for the hazard-insurance thresholds. This is the section that turns an approval into a list of things that must happen, and it applies to SBA business loans rather than to private funding.

readings.title: CFPB - Regulation B, 12 CFR 1002.2 (definitions, including adverse action)
readings.note: Read the definition of adverse action, in particular the counteroffer carve-out in 1002.2(c)(1)(i): a refusal to grant credit in substantially the amount or on substantially the terms requested is adverse action unless the creditor makes a counteroffer and the applicant uses or expressly accepts the credit offered. Read also the exclusions in 1002.2(c)(2). Whether the regulation's business-credit provisions reach a particular applicant is a legal question.

readings.title: SBA - SBA lenders and business loan program comparison
readings.note: Read the program comparison table for the published size and maturity boundaries of 7(a), CDC/504 and Microloan, and read the lender eligibility requirements to see what SBA expects of a lender before it may issue a guaranteed loan. Useful context for the sentence that an approval is the funder's or SBA's decision, never the advisor's.

visual.title: Reading a conditional offer in four passes
visual.description: A labelled sequence for turning an offer letter and a counteroffer into a comparison a merchant can check, a conditions list a merchant can clear, and an accurate description of the file's legal status.
steps: Step 1, read the amount and the tail: total repayment, the remittance and its cadence, and the number of payments, stated as figures rather than as adjectives.

Step 2, compute cost on the right denominator: total repayment divided by net proceeds after fees, expressed as dollars per $100 of net proceeds, and separately as a percentage of the merchant's weekly contribution.
Step 3, compare the counteroffer on three axes at once: amount, duration and cost per dollar, because smaller and shorter often arrives with a higher cost on the same page.

Step 4, write the conditions list with a date against each item, including guarantees, appraisals, insurance, payoff letters and any condition the letter does not name, and mark that no funds have moved.

Step 5, name the legal event precisely: an accepted counteroffer is carved out of the adverse action definition, a refusal in substantially the amount or terms requested is not, and either way the notification question is answered by the regulation and by counsel, not by the advisor.

questions.prompt: A provider sends a merchant in a state whose list you have not read a disclosure with five numbered lines. You have previously audited offers in another state whose list has six. Before saying anything to the merchant, what is the correct first move, and what will you count?
questions.answer: Fetch the current numbered list from the governing state's disclosure section, count the items there, and audit the document against that list, noting which rows are conditional and which are due at the offer; a five-line document cannot be scored against a six-item list from a different state.
questions.distractor: Audit the five lines against the six-item list you already know, mark the missing item as a defect, and tell the merchant the offer is incomplete pending that line.
questions.correction: Item lists belong to jurisdictions, not to products, so scoring one state's document against another state's list produces both false gaps and false passes. The correct method is to open the governing state's section, write its numbered items as rows before reading the document, mark conditional rows as conditional, and then report presence, error or absence per row together with the count as a fraction of origination items. The two lists genuinely differ: in the pair used in this level, the two statutes produce fifteen item slots describing eleven distinct requirements, with the annualized-rate item appearing in one list and broker compensation, collateral, other potential fees, the estimated number of payments and the total repayment amount appearing only in the other.

questions.prompt: A merchant asks whether the annualized rate printed on a disclosure from a disclosure-law state is the same thing as an APR, and whether you can therefore quote a comparable annual figure for a factor-based advance alongside it.
questions.answer: No: a statutory annualized rate is a defined disclosure term produced under that state's method, an APR is a different construct from a different regime with its own rules, and a factor is a multiplier applied to an advance rather than a rate; the honest answer describes the disclosed figure as what the statute requires and refuses to convert the factor into an annual figure.
questions.distractor: Yes, both are annualised cost measures, so the advisor can convert the factor into an equivalent annual rate and present the two figures side by side for comparison.
questions.correction: Treating one state's annualized-rate item as an APR collapses three different things: a disclosure term defined by a statute, an annual percentage rate defined in consumer credit rules, and a factor that prices a purchase of receivables or an advance. The lesson's rule is the honesty rule this course applies throughout: a factor is not a rate and is never described as an APR. What the advisor may do is state the commercial cost in the terms the documents actually use, dollars of total repayment per $100 of net proceeds, total repayment, the remittance and its cadence, and any disclosed annualized figure as the state defines it, each with its own label.

questions.prompt: A contract allows prepayment and states the total repayment amount, and it says nothing further about early payoff. The merchant plans to finish in week 10 of 24 on a $48,000 advance at a factor of 1.34 and expects to save the unearned portion. Write the correct read.
questions.answer: Silence about prepayment means the scheduled remaining balance is owed, so the payoff at week 10 is the $37,520.00 remaining of the $64,320.00 total, and the early finish saves time rather than dollars; state both the balance and the weeks removed, and note that a discount or penalty clause would change the figure.
questions.distractor: Prepaying saves the finance charge that has not yet been earned, so the advisor should prorate the $16,320.00 of cost over the unused 14 weeks and quote a payoff of about the principal remaining.
questions.correction: A saving exists only where a clause creates one, and prorating a factor as though it were accruing interest imports a consumer loan assumption into a purchase of receivables. Where a clause does price prepayment, the arithmetic is explicit and runs on the remaining scheduled balance: a 3 percent discount on $37,520.00 is $1,125.60, a payoff of $36,394.40, which is 3.00 percent of the remaining balance and 1.75 percent of the total repayment. Both percentages belong in the sentence because they are both true and a merchant will otherwise hear only the friendlier one.

questions.prompt: A folder for a merchant contains a financing statement filed 2019-08-02 covering all assets, a search dated today showing no continuation, a filing from 2024 covering inventory, and a bankruptcy petition filed four days ago by the business. The merchant wants to know whether the funder can still collect this week and whether the business is unencumbered. Write the two answers.
questions.answer: Collection is barred as to collection acts because a petition operates as a stay applicable to all entities and reaches acts to collect a pre-petition claim, so the funder's scheduled debit is a collection act regardless of the contract; and the business is not shown to be unencumbered, because the 2019-08-02 all-assets filing lapsed on 2024-08-02 unless continued within the window that closed on that date, which addresses UCC priority rather than the amount owed.
questions.distractor: The business is unencumbered because the blanket filing lapsed with no continuation, and the funder can keep collecting because the contract signed by the merchant authorises the debits.
questions.correction: Two separate errors appear in that sentence. A lapse unperfecteds the security interest and, as against a purchaser of the collateral for value, unwinds it retroactively, but the underlying obligation is a different question that no search answers; the record must be read as dates and collateral lines with an explicit not-proved column. And the stay is statutory rather than contractual, so it binds all entities and reaches collection acts by operation of law, which means a contract's debit authorisation does not set it aside. The advisor states what the filings prove, dates the lapse, and refers the legal question rather than answering it.

questions.prompt: A merchant supplies a cash-method return showing $96,400 of net profit, a bank statement showing $468,000 of deposits, and a note that $58,000 of December invoices were collected in January. He asks how much weekly payment the business can carry. What must the advisor produce before answering, and what are the key figures?
questions.answer: A reconciliation and a cash rebuild: $412,000 of receipts plus $40,000 of loan proceeds plus $9,500 of owner contribution plus $6,500 of returned deposit equals $468,000 of deposits exactly; and $96,400 plus $14,800 of depreciation minus $62,400 of principal payments minus $48,000 of owner draws equals $800.00 of free cash, with the $58,000 of December receipts and any section 481(a) amount listed separately as timing facts.
questions.distractor: Use the $468,000 of deposits as the revenue base, subtract the merchant's stated monthly expenses, and treat the remaining margin as capacity, since deposits are the cash the business actually handled.
questions.correction: Deposits are not revenue and net profit is not cash. Deposits include loan proceeds, owner contributions and refunds, and the reconciliation strips them out to reach $412,000 of receipts; the cash rebuild then removes non-cash deductions by adding depreciation back, and removes cash that is not an expense by subtracting principal payments and draws. The result, $800.00, differs from the headline by $95,600, so a capacity figure built on the headline overstates by more than a hundredfold on this file. The $58,000 collected in January is a timing difference that a cash-basis return legitimately omits, and a section 481(a) amount belongs to an earlier period rather than to this year's trading.

units.title: Producing the artifacts: the comparison sheet, the evidence calendar, truthful outreach, the counterparty file and the auditable packet

lessons.title: Producing a one-page cost comparison the merchant can check with a calculator
lessons.explanation: The comparison sheet is the deliverable this level exists to produce, and its design is a control rather than a sales aid. Every row must be traceable to a document with a date, every percentage must name its base, and every figure must be reproducible by the merchant on a calculator. The rows are fixed: the gross amount; each fee deducted or withheld at disbursement, listed separately; the net proceeds; the total repayment; the remittance and its cadence; the total repayment expressed as dollars per $100 of net proceeds; the remittance expressed as a percentage of the merchant's contribution on the same cadence; the first and last scheduled payment dates; the prepayment terms read from the clause; the security and guarantee position; and the disclosure items present for the governing jurisdiction. There is no rate column, because a factor is a multiplier rather than a rate and this sheet never converts one into an annual percentage rate. There is no winner column, because the sheet's job is to make the arithmetic legible, not to rank instruments for a merchant whose working capital and risk appetite the advisor does not own. Two denominators are stated separately because using one alone misleads: the financing amount makes a factor look smaller, and the net proceeds is the money the merchant actually receives. The sheet therefore reports dollars per $100 of net proceeds, which is larger than the factor, and it says so in a footnote rather than leaving the difference to be discovered. A rounding convention belongs on the page as well: when a weekly remittance does not divide evenly, the final payment differs by cents, and the sheet names the difference instead of hiding it. Finally, the sheet carries three sentences that no spreadsheet can generate: the timing assumptions, the preparer's own compensation, and what the merchant still has to clear before anything is funded.
lessons.example: Two offers for the same merchant, whose weekly contribution is $12,400. Offer A is a $60,000 advance at a factor of 1.35 repaid over 26 weekly payments, with a 4.5 percent origination fee deducted at disbursement and a $895 administrative fee. The sheet computes: total repayment $60,000 times 1.35 is $81,000.00; the weekly remittance is $81,000.00 divided by 26, or $3,115.38; fees of $2,700.00 and $895.00 leave net proceeds of $56,405.00; and $81,000.00 divided by $56,405.00 is $143.60 per $100 of net proceeds against a nominal factor of 1.35. The remittance is 25.12 percent of the weekly contribution, and the same arithmetic on a monthly base gives $13,500.00 a month against $53,733.33 of monthly contribution, which is the same 25.12 percent and is why the base must be named. Offer B is a $60,000 term loan over 48 months at an illustrative nominal 10.25 percent with a $1,200.00 origination fee. The monthly payment is $1,528.97; total payments are $73,390.56; interest is $13,390.56; net proceeds are $58,800.00; and total payments divided by net proceeds is $124.81 per $100 of net proceeds. The monthly payment is 2.85 percent of monthly contribution. The sheet shows both rows side by side and states three facts that follow from them without ranking them. Offer A costs $18.79 more per $100 of net proceeds, which is 15.05 percent more on that measure, and finishes in about six months rather than 48. Offer A consumes 25.12 percent of monthly contribution against 2.85 percent for B. And the two measures are not the same instrument: one is a purchase of receivables priced by a factor and the other is an amortising loan priced by a nominal rate, so the sheet refuses to line the metrics up and says so in the footnote. The rounding line reads: 26 payments of $3,115.38 total $80,999.88, so the final payment is trued up by $0.12 to make $81,000.00 exactly.
lessons.question: A merchant says the second offer is cheaper because its payment is smaller. What does the comparison sheet show, and what does the advisor say?
lessons.answer: The monthly payments are $13,500.00 for the advance and $1,528.97 for the term loan, so the smaller payment belongs to the longer, differently priced instrument; on the same measure of total repayment per $100 of net proceeds the advance is $143.60 and the term loan is $124.81, and the advisor presents both rows with their cadences, tails and bases rather than declaring a cheaper offer.
lessons.distractor: The term loan is cheaper on every measure, since $1,528.97 a month is far below $13,500.00 a month and the total repayment is also lower, so the advisor should recommend it and note the longer term as the only trade-off.
lessons.correction: Comparing a monthly payment with a monthly equivalent is legitimate and shows what the merchant's cash flow will feel like; comparing total repayment with total repayment is also legitimate because both figures are stated. What is not legitimate is concluding that one instrument is cheaper when they are priced on different bases: $124.81 per $100 of net proceeds is lower than $143.60, and 48 months carries four years of exposure that a six-month obligation does not. The sheet's purpose is to make both facts visible in one place, with the timing assumptions and the preparer's compensation stated on the page, and to leave the ranking to the merchant, who owns the working capital decision.

depth.definitions: Net proceeds are the gross amount less every fee deducted or withheld at disbursement, which is why a fee not listed cannot be verified and must be treated as absent evidence rather than as zero. The per-$100-of-net-proceeds measure divides total repayment by net proceeds and multiplies by 100; it is deliberately larger than a factor because its denominator is smaller than the gross amount, and the label states the denominator so that no reader has to guess. Cadence is the rhythm of the remittance, weekly, bi-weekly, semi-monthly, monthly, or share-of-receipts with a reconciliation, and no percentage comparison is valid across different cadences unless both figures are converted to the same period. The contribution base is the merchant's cash available to service the obligation over the same period, and it must be named with its source. A traceable figure is one the merchant can reach from a document with a date using only addition, subtraction, multiplication and division. The sheet's closing lines are part of its definition as an artifact: timing assumptions, preparer compensation, and the open conditions. Scope: this sheet is an educational work product and not a disclosure document under any state regime, and where a jurisdiction requires a specific form or item list, that form governs.
depth.mechanism: The sheet changes outcomes through four mechanisms. It constrains the preparer, because a figure that cannot be traced to a document cannot be entered, and a fee the preparer would rather bury must be listed to compute net proceeds. It forces the base of every percentage into the open, which is the single most effective defence against the flattering comparison; the same deal reads as 1.35, as 143.60 per $100 of net proceeds, and as 25.12 percent of contribution, and all three are true. It converts the conversation from trust to arithmetic: a merchant who can reproduce a row with a calculator is checking the advisor rather than believing the advisor, which is the correct relationship for a decision of this size. And it produces a record, so that if the merchant later says the advisor promised a result, the document shows what was actually presented, including the preparer's compensation and the open conditions. The rounding convention belongs to the same mechanism: a sheet that admits a $0.12 true-up on the final payment is a sheet whose other figures are more likely to be trusted, because it demonstrates that the author reconciled rather than rounded toward a conclusion.
depth.secondExample: A third offer with a reconciliation clause shows how the sheet changes shape rather than how it changes rules. The offer quotes a fixed weekly remittance with periodic true-up against a percentage of receipts, so the completion date is a range and the sheet's last-payment row reads as an estimate with a note naming what determines it: the receipts actually collected. The other rows are unchanged, and the per-$100 measure is computed on the same base, with one added line stating that the range, not the estimate, is what the merchant should plan against. A fourth variant moves who pays the broker: when the provider pays the broker's compensation, the merchant's net proceeds are untouched and the sheet records the payment as a compensation line rather than a fee, which is exactly the item that a statutory disclosure list in at least one state requires the provider to state. In both variants the sheet's value comes from the columns it refuses to add. There is still no rate column, no winner column, and no column for an annual figure built by converting a factor, because none of those columns can be computed from the documents the merchant actually holds.
depth.mistake: The first error is comparing payments across cadences without converting: $1,528.97 a month against $3,115.38 a week is not a comparison at all, and the honest conversion puts the advance at $13,500.00 a month, which is 25.12 percent of the merchant's monthly contribution. The second is leaving a fee out of net proceeds, which flatters the per-$100 measure and cannot be caught later because the missing fee never appears. The third is adding a rate column and converting a factor into an annual figure, which this course prohibits: a factor is not a rate and is not described as an APR, and a sheet that invents an annualised column has manufactured a number no document supports. The diagnostic is quick: hand the sheet to a colleague with a calculator and ask them to reproduce three random cells from the source documents. Every cell they cannot reach from a dated document is a cell that does not belong on the page.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Build a one-page comparison sheet for two real or provided offers with the fixed rows listed in the lesson, then have another person attempt to reproduce three cells from the source documents without help. Model response: for the worked pair, the sheet shows Offer A at $81,000.00 of total repayment, $3,115.38 weekly, $56,405.00 of net proceeds, $143.60 per $100 of net proceeds, 25.12 percent of contribution, a six-month tail, a 4.5 percent fee and an $895 administrative fee itemized, and a $0.12 final-payment true-up; Offer B at $73,390.56 of total payments, $1,528.97 monthly, $58,800.00 of net proceeds, $124.81 per $100 of net proceeds, 2.85 percent of contribution, a 48-month tail, and $13,390.56 of interest on an illustrative nominal rate; plus a footnote stating that the two instruments are priced on different bases and cannot be lined up, a compensation line, and the open conditions. Rubric: three points for every fee itemized into net proceeds; three for the two cost measures with named bases; two for cadence conversion; two for the timing footnote and compensation line; two for reproducing the rounding difference rather than rounding it away. A sheet with an unstated denominator, a missing fee, or a converted annual percentage rate cannot pass.
depth.summary: A comparison sheet is an accountability artifact. It fixes the rows in advance, itemises every fee into net proceeds, states two cost measures with their denominators, converts cadences honestly, names a rounding difference instead of hiding it, and closes with timing assumptions, the preparer's compensation and the conditions still open. What it does not do is rank the offers, invent a rate, or resolve the merchant's cash-flow decision, which belongs to the merchant with the advisor's arithmetic in hand.

readings.title: Code of Virginia, section 6.2-2231 - Disclosure requirements
readings.note: Read the nine items as a checklist for the sheet's disclosure column: the disbursement amount after fees deducted or withheld at disbursement, the finance charge, the total repayment amount defined as the disbursement amount plus the finance charge, the payment amounts and frequency, other potential fees, and the broker-compensation line. Each item maps to a row or footnote on a well-built sheet.

readings.title: California Financial Code, section 22802 - Commercial financing disclosures
readings.note: Read subdivision (b) to see which items a disclosure in that state must carry, including the total cost expressed as an annualized rate, and subdivision (a) for the signature step. Use it to keep the sheet's footnotes honest about what a state's own form requires as distinct from what the advisor chooses to present.

readings.title: SBA - SBA lenders and business loan program comparison
readings.note: Read the program comparison table for the published size and maturity boundaries of 7(a), CDC/504 and Microloan. Useful when a sheet's rows include a guaranteed product, because the row's maturity and amount have to sit inside the programme's stated boundaries rather than inside the advisor's assumption.

visual.title: The twelve rows of a checkable comparison sheet
visual.description: A labelled layout sequence showing what each row of the sheet must contain and which rows a merchant can verify unaided.
steps: Step 1, fix the identity block: merchant, date, preparer, the governing jurisdiction, and the preparer's own compensation stated in dollars.
Step 2, build the money rows from documents: gross amount, each fee deducted at disbursement listed separately, net proceeds, total repayment, and the remittance with its cadence.
Step 3, add the two cost measures with named denominators: dollars per $100 of net proceeds, and the remittance as a percentage of contribution converted to the same period.

Step 4, add the time and risk rows: first and last scheduled payment dates, the prepayment clause read in its own words, the security and guarantee position, and which disclosure items are present for the jurisdiction.

Step 5, close with the three prose lines: timing assumptions including any reconciliation clause, the rounding difference on the final payment, and the conditions the merchant must still clear before funding.

lessons.title: Producing an evidence calendar and a document-collection log
lessons.explanation: A funding file is decided by documents, and documents have periods, sources, validity windows and versions, which is why the second artifact of this level is a calendar rather than a folder. The design has four rules. First, one row per document per period: twelve monthly statements are twelve rows, not one row called statements, because a single row cannot show which month is missing and cannot carry a date. Second, every document type carries a validity window, written before collection begins rather than argued after: a bank or processor statement dated within the last 45 days is current, a payoff letter dated within 14 days is current, a UCC search run within 30 days is current, and an insurance certificate is current for its policy period. Third, every row carries five fields, which for a twelve-document set is sixty cells: the period covered, the source, the date requested, the date received, and the status (current, stale, superseded or missing). Fourth, versions are kept rather than replaced, and the log records which version was relied upon and on what date, because the question a reviewer asks is not whether a document exists but which document the recommendation rested on. The calendar matters for three reasons that have nothing to do with tidiness. It makes absence visible and dated, so a missing statement is a row and a number rather than a vague concern. It separates stale from missing: a statement for the right period supplied eleven months late is a different problem from a statement that was never supplied, and only a dated log shows which one is in front of you. And it converts a chase into a schedule, which changes the advisor's own conduct: instead of repeated requests, the calendar states what is due, from whom, by when, and what the consequence of lateness is, so the merchant can see the cost of delay rather than experiencing it as pressure.
lessons.example: A working file for a merchant whose reconciliation clause requires monthly statements. The request goes out on 2026-10-05 for twelve monthly statements plus a payoff letter for an existing obligation and a fresh search. The first pass is due 2026-10-10. Everything received is dated on arrival. The log records that the earliest statement is for the period ending 2025-11-30, which on the reading date of 2026-10-05 is 309 days old, that is 264 days beyond a 45-day current window, so that row is marked stale rather than missing. Two months in the middle of the year arrive twice, once as a processor PDF and once as a bank statement, so both rows carry the version field and the log states which one was relied upon and when. The payoff letter is requested from the existing funder on 2026-10-05 and is only useful for 14 days, so its row has an expiry date built in, and if it arrives on 2026-10-20 it must be refreshed before it supports anything. The cost accounting is explicit, because it is the argument for building the calendar at all. Three collection rounds of twelve messages at six minutes each is 216 minutes, or 3.6 hours, which at $95.00 an hour is $342.00. The merchant's own time, twelve documents at twenty minutes each, is four hours, which at $65.00 is $260.00. A nine-day delay in assembling the file costs nine days of deferred deployment at $180.00 a day, which is $1,620.00. The three figures sum to $2,222.00, and the calendar's purpose is to make that number smaller, not to document that it happened. The log's summary line reads: twelve periods requested, nine current, one stale, two missing, one payoff letter with a 14-day window, one search with a 30-day window, sixty cells tracked.
lessons.question: A merchant supplies a statement for the correct period that is eleven months old, and another that he never supplied. Should both be treated the same way, and how does the calendar record them?
lessons.answer: No: the old statement is a stale row with a known period, which can often be used for context but not as current evidence, while the unsupplied statement is a missing row that blocks the same way an absent document blocks; the calendar records each as its own row with its own status so that the two problems are not averaged into one.
lessons.distractor: Both are documentation gaps, so the log marks the set as incomplete and the advisor requests the whole twelve months again, which keeps the record simple and avoids arguing about individual periods.
lessons.correction: Averaging a stale document and an absent document destroys the information the calendar exists to hold. A stale row tells the advisor that the business did trade in that period and that the evidence is older than the window; a missing row tells the advisor that nothing is known about that period. Re-requesting twelve months when one is absent also wastes the merchant's time, which has a dollar value the lesson computes at $65.00 an hour. The correct log records per-period status, keeps both versions when a document arrives twice and names the one relied upon with a date, and attaches the expiry date to documents with short windows such as payoff letters and searches, so that a document can be current on one date and stale on another without anyone having to remember.

depth.definitions: An evidence calendar is a dated schedule of documents by period, source and status. A collection log is the record of who was asked, when, what arrived and when. A validity window is the period during which a document type is treated as current, set in advance: statements 45 days, payoff letters 14 days, UCC searches 30 days, insurance certificates for the policy period. A stale document is one whose period is correct but whose age exceeds the window; a superseded document is one replaced by a later version and retained; a missing document is one with no row content at all. A version is one rendering of the same period's evidence, and the relied-upon version is the one named in the recommendation. Retention is a separate rule set: the Internal Revenue Service's guidance states that records must be kept as long as needed to prove the income or deductions on a return, that the responsibility to substantiate is the taxpayer's burden of proof, and that employment tax records should be kept at least four years; and for business credit, the regulation's record-retention provisions set periods that vary with the applicant's gross revenues, including a special rule for business credit where gross revenues exceed $1 million or where the credit is trade credit or credit incident to a factoring agreement, with the period extended on a written request. Scope: retention rules attach to particular parties and categories, so an advisor keeps records for their own reasons and does not speak for the merchant's tax position.
depth.mechanism: The calendar works because it changes what is arguable. A folder makes absence a matter of memory and a chase a matter of persistence; a calendar makes both into rows with dates, and a row can be counted. Three mechanisms follow. First, dating creates a decay curve: because a statement describes a period rather than a moment, its evidential value falls as the period recedes, and a window written in advance converts that judgement into a status a second person can reproduce. Second, separating stale from missing preserves two different facts, one about the business and one about the file, and treating them alike either wastes the merchant's time or hides the gap. Third, versioning protects the recommendation: when the same period arrives twice with different numbers, the log's relied-upon line is the only record of what the arithmetic was built on, and without it the advisor cannot reconstruct their own reasoning, which is precisely the failure documented in the earlier level's documentation lesson. The cost of collection is part of the mechanism rather than an afterthought, because a calendar that shortens delay has a measurable value, and stating that value in dollars is what persuades a merchant to participate in the schedule.
depth.secondExample: The same artifact built for a file with a true-up shows how the period structure changes. Because the obligation is reconciled against a percentage of receipts, the statement set must be refreshed rather than collected once, so the calendar has a recurring block: one row per month per document type, with the next refresh date and the reconciliation date named in advance. A second file shows the source column doing real work: the funder requires the merchant to submit statements directly to a portal, so the advisor never touches the documents and the log's role changes from collection to verification, recording that the portal received a statement for each period and that the figures the advisor used match what the merchant uploaded. In both variants the rules are unchanged: one row per period, a window per type, five fields per row, versions retained and one named. What changes is who holds the source, and the log is the place where that difference is recorded so that a reviewer can see it.
depth.mistake: The first error is the single summary row: one line reading statements received collapses twelve periods into a claim and cannot show which month is missing. The second is treating a stale document as usable because it covers a real period; its period is real and its evidence is old, and stating it as current overstates the file. The third is discarding superseded versions, which destroys the ability to reconstruct what was relied upon when a later version changes a number. The fourth is confusing retention with currency: keeping a document for years says nothing about whether it was current on the date of the decision, and an advisor who says the file is compliant because documents were retained has answered a different question. The diagnostic is the sixty-cell test: twelve rows times five fields, every cell filled with a value or explicitly marked missing, with the relied-upon version named in a date-stamped line.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Build an evidence calendar for one file with at least three document types and twelve statement periods, fill all five fields per row, compute the status counts, and write the cost-of-collection lines. Model response: twelve statement rows with periods, sources, request dates, receipt dates and statuses yielding nine current, one stale and two missing; a payoff-letter row with a 14-day window and an expiry date; a search row with a 30-day window; a version line naming which duplicate was relied upon and on which date; and cost lines of $342.00 for the advisor's three collection rounds, $260.00 for the merchant's four hours, and $1,620.00 for a nine-day delay, totalling $2,222.00. Rubric: three points for one row per period with all five fields; two for the stale-versus-missing distinction; two for version control with a relied-upon line; two for dates attached to short-window documents; one for the cost arithmetic. A calendar with a summary row in place of per-period rows, or with no expiry on the payoff letter, cannot pass.
depth.summary: Documents are managed by period, source, window and version, and the calendar is the artifact that makes all four countable. It makes absence a row rather than a feeling, keeps stale and missing apart, preserves the version that supported the arithmetic, and gives the cost of delay a dollar figure the merchant can weigh. Retention and currency stay separate in the reader's mind, and the log stays silent about tax positions that belong to the merchant's preparer.

lessons.title: Producing truthful outreach: claims, email, fax and text under the advertising and contact rules
lessons.explanation: Outreach is where an advisor's claims become the firm's claims, and the artifact to produce is a piece of text plus a claim table that shows why every sentence in it can stand. The FTC's own summary of the truth-in-advertising rules states three: advertising must be truthful and non-deceptive; advertisers must have evidence to back up their claims; and advertisements cannot be unfair. Deception is a likelihood question about a statement or omission that would mislead a reasonable person acting reasonably in the circumstances, and materiality means it is likely to affect conduct or a decision, which is why an omitted fee sits in the same analysis as a stated guarantee. Substantiation is a documentation duty rather than a belief: the evidence has to be in hand before the claim runs. Then the channel rules attach, and they differ by channel. Email: 15 U.S.C. section 7704(a)(5) requires three elements in a commercial electronic mail message, clear and conspicuous identification that the message is an advertisement or solicitation, with an exception where the recipient has given prior affirmative consent, clear and conspicuous notice of the opportunity to decline further messages, and a valid physical postal address of the sender. Section 7704(a)(3) requires an opt-out mechanism that remains capable of receiving requests for no less than 30 days after the transmission, and section 7704(a)(4) makes it unlawful to send a message within the scope of a request more than 10 business days after receiving it, and unlawful to sell, lease, exchange or otherwise transfer the address of a person who made such a request except to comply with the law, subject to a subsequent-consent exception. Note the two clocks and their units: thirty days is the life of the mechanism, ten business days is the deadline to honour a request, and business days are not calendar days. Fax: 47 CFR 64.1200(a)(4) makes an unsolicited advertisement to a fax machine unlawful unless the sender has an established business relationship with the recipient, obtained the number either from the recipient directly within that relationship or from a source the recipient voluntarily made public for public distribution, and the advertisement carries a clear and conspicuous notice on its first page describing how to request no further advertisements; a complying request must be honoured within the shortest reasonable time, not exceeding 30 days. Texts and calls: 47 CFR 64.1200(a)(1)(iii) covers telephone numbers assigned to cellular services, and (a)(2) requires prior express written consent for telemarketing calls made with an automatic telephone dialing system or an artificial or prerecorded voice to those numbers. These provisions are read here to show what an outreach artifact must contain; whether a particular campaign is covered, and by which rule, is a compliance question for counsel.
lessons.example: A draft outreach email and its claim table. The draft reads: approved funding in 24 hours, guaranteed $75,000 for your business, SBA-backed rates, only three spots left this week, and a click-through button. The claim table lists fourteen statements a reader could treat as factual, and the audit sorts them into five deleted, four rewritten and five kept. Deleted: guaranteed $75,000, because an amount cannot be guaranteed before underwriting; SBA-backed, because the sentence implies an affiliation that does not exist and this course prohibits false affiliations outright; the three-spots scarcity line, because nothing in the file establishes a limit; the 24-hour approval claim; and one testimonial sentence sourced to nobody. Rewritten: the turnaround claim becomes a statement that the funder's own stated timeline will be provided in writing before any application, sourced to that funder's published terms rather than to the advisor's optimism; the amount becomes the range the merchant's documents could support, expressed as a range with the evidence named; a cost phrase becomes total repayment in dollars per $100 of net proceeds with the denominator named; and a comparison against another funder becomes a comparison against the merchant's request rather than against a competitor. Kept: the sender's identity, the physical postal address, the opt-out mechanism, and two factual sentences about what happens next. That is five deleted of fourteen, or 35.71 percent, and the re-check of the remaining nine passes nine of nine. The footer is then tested rather than assumed: the opt-out link is clicked on day one and again on day thirty-one, because section 7704(a)(3) requires the mechanism to remain capable for no less than 30 days, and the physical address is verified because section 7704(a)(5) requires a valid one. Before the send, 480 addresses are checked against a suppression list of 62 entries, and every reply is logged with its date. The planning line states the observed reply range in a test batch of 50 per variant, which at 2.1 percent is 10.08 replies per 480 and at 1.6 percent is 7.68, and it states those as observations with their batch size rather than as a forecast. Nowhere does the artifact include a deadline that is not in a document with a date.
lessons.question: A colleague wants to keep the line 'SBA-backed rates' because the funder holds an SBA lender participation agreement for another product line. What is the correct decision, and what is the reason?
lessons.answer: Delete the line: it implies an affiliation between the advisor's or funder's offer and SBA that the offer does not carry, and a truthful claim would have to name the programme, the participating lender and the guarantee structure as they actually apply to this merchant's file, which is a statement the affiliate product line cannot support.
lessons.distractor: Keep the line but add the word 'eligible' so it reads as SBA-eligible rates, since the funder does hold an SBA participation agreement and the merchant merely has to qualify for that product.
lessons.correction: The problem is not one word; it is a claim of association that the specific offer does not have. A truthful version names an actual programme with its actual terms, or says nothing about SBA at all. The same test applies to every claim in the table: can the evidence be produced from a document with a date, and does the sentence mean what the reader will take it to mean. The affiliate product line answers a different question, and neither the guarantee of approval nor the implication of a government connection survives an audit that asks for the document behind the sentence.

depth.definitions: A claim is a statement a reader could treat as a factual assertion about a product, a price, an outcome, a timeline or a person. Substantiation is the evidence held before the claim is published. Deception is a representation, omission or practice likely to mislead a reasonable person in the circumstances, where materiality means it is likely to affect conduct or a decision. An unsolicited advertisement is an advertisement sent without the recipient's prior permission, defined in the covered-channel rules; an established business relationship is a defined status in the telemarketing rules rather than a general impression of familiarity. An opt-out mechanism is the means by which a recipient declines further messages, and prior affirmative consent is a recipient's agreement in advance, which for some campaigns and some technologies must be written. A suppression list is the set of addresses and numbers that must not be contacted, checked before each send. Business days are not calendar days, a distinction that changes the deadline for honouring an email opt-out request. Two scope notes: the FTC's advertising summary is about advertising generally rather than about business funding specifically, and the channel rules apply according to the technology used, the recipient and the purpose, which is a compliance question for counsel.
depth.mechanism: Four mechanisms make this artifact different from a marketing draft. First, substantiation is a documentation duty, which means the claim table is written before the copy rather than after a complaint, and any claim lacking a document is deleted rather than softened. Second, the email rules create maintenance obligations rather than one-time settings: the opt-out mechanism must remain capable for at least 30 days after each transmission and requests must be honoured within 10 business days, so a dead link or an unattended inbox is a violation of the same provision that required the link. Third, the fax rule's placement requirement follows from where a decision is made: the notice must be clear and conspicuous on the first page, because a recipient decides from the page in hand, and the exemption depends on how the number was obtained, which is a fact the sender must be able to document. Fourth, suppression is list control, and the burden sits with the sender even when a list was purchased or a platform sent the message, which is why the record names the list version and the check date. Together these mechanisms explain why outreach is a production discipline: the artifact is not judged on its tone but on whether each sentence has a document behind it and each channel has its required elements.
depth.secondExample: The same artifact built for a different channel produces a different required set, which is the point of producing it channel by channel. For a text or call campaign to mobile numbers, section 64.1200(a)(2) requires prior express written consent for telemarketing calls made with an automatic telephone dialing system or an artificial or prerecorded voice to numbers assigned to cellular services, so the artifact includes the consent record with its date rather than an opt-out line, and the suppression check runs against the do-not-call machinery as well. For a fax to a business, the artifact includes the established business relationship with the recipient, the documented source of the number within one of the permitted ways, and the first-page notice, and the honouring window is the shortest reasonable time not exceeding 30 days. For an email to a merchant who previously asked for information, the required set is the three elements of section 7704(a)(5), and the consent exception applies only to the identification element. Three channels, three checklists, one method: write the claim table, list the required elements for the channel actually being used, and test the mechanism on a later date rather than on the day it was built.
depth.mistake: The first error is importing copy from another vertical where different rules apply, which is how consumer-style promises end up in business funding outreach. The second is treating a footer as compliance: an opt-out line that leads nowhere, or an address that was never verified, fails the requirement it was meant to satisfy, and the thirty-day capability test is designed to catch exactly that. The third is assuming that an existing contact may be contacted without a mechanism, when the email rule requires notice of the opportunity to decline and the fax rule requires a first-page notice even inside an established business relationship. The fourth is manufactured urgency: a deadline or a scarcity line is only usable when a document with a date establishes it, and a deadline invented to speed a decision is the same conduct in a milder form as the deceptive practices the enforcement record describes. The diagnostic is to read the artifact as a stranger would and mark every sentence that is a claim, then mark whether the evidence is in the file today. Any claim without evidence is deleted, not toned down.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Take one real or drafted outreach piece, build its claim table, then produce the corrected version with the required channel elements and a test of the opt-out mechanism on a later date. Model response: fourteen claims identified; five deleted, including a guaranteed amount, an implied association, and an unsupported scarcity line; four rewritten with named sources or denominators; five kept, including identity, postal address and the opt-out mechanism; three required email elements present; the mechanism tested on day one and day thirty-one; 480 addresses checked against 62 suppressed entries before the send; and a planning line stating observed reply rates of 10.08 and 7.68 responses per batch of 480 with the test batch size named. Rubric: three points for the claim table with a decision and a reason per claim; three for the channel's required elements; two for testing the opt-out mechanism after the thirty-day threshold rather than on the first day; one for the suppression check with its date; one for stating rates as observations with batch size. An artifact that keeps an approval guarantee, implies an affiliation, or relies on an untested opt-out link cannot pass.
depth.summary: Outreach is authored backwards: the claim table first, the required channel elements second, the copy third. Truthfulness is a documentation condition rather than a tone, the email, fax and texting provisions add specific elements and clocks, and suppression is a list operation with the burden on the sender. What the artifact must never contain is a promise of approval, an implied affiliation, an inventory or deadline that no document establishes, or a hidden cost, and the test that catches all four is a single question asked of every sentence: where is the document, and when was it dated.

visual.title: Authoring outreach from the claim table outward
visual.description: A labelled sequence that produces a truthful outreach artifact by deciding on claims before writing copy and by testing the mechanism after it is built.
steps: Step 1, list every factual claim the draft makes about price, amount, timing, outcome, affiliation or availability, and write the evidence beside each one with its date.
Step 2, decide per claim: delete what has no evidence, rewrite what can be sourced, keep what is already true and demonstrated.

Step 3, add the required elements for the channel actually used, including identification, notice of the opt-out opportunity and a valid physical postal address for email, or the first-page notice and number-source documentation for a fax.

lessons.title: Producing a counterparty vetting file before you send a merchant anywhere
lessons.explanation: A merchant cannot check a funder, and an advisor who has not checked one is passing an unknown counterparty into a decision that will bind the business for months. The vetting file is the artifact that replaces an impression with documented facts, and it groups into four kinds of check. Registration comes first because in some states permission is a precondition. Virginia requires every sales-based financing provider and broker to register with the State Corporation Commission, requires the application to disclose any judgment, memorandum of understanding, cease and desist order or conviction involving a crime, fraud, breach of trust or money laundering as to that person or any officer, director, manager, operator or individual who otherwise controls its operations, charges a $1,000 initial registration fee and a $500 annual fee due by September 15, and provides that a failure to pay the annual fee makes the registration expire automatically by operation of law. Utah states that it is unlawful for a person to engage in a commercial financing transaction as a provider in Utah or with a Utah resident without registering with the Department and maintaining a valid registration. Status comes second, because programme claims are checkable. Where an SBA product is discussed, the published 7(a) participation requirements are four countable criteria: a continuing ability to evaluate, process, close, disburse, service and liquidate small business loans; being open to the public to issue loans and not a financing subsidiary engaged primarily in financing the operations of an affiliate; continuing good character and reputation and the ethical requirements identified in 13 CFR part 120.140; and supervision and examination by a state or federal regulatory authority satisfactory to SBA, or application as a Small Business Lending Company or Non-Federally Regulated Lender under SOP 50 56. Conduct comes third, and the enforcement record is a source of specific check items rather than a general caution. The FTC announced on January 5, 2022 that two defendants behind an alleged small business financing scheme, RAM Capital Funding, LLC and its owner Tzvi Reich, would be permanently banned from the merchant cash advance and debt collection industries and required to pay $675,000 to settle charges that they used deceptive and illegal means to seize assets from small businesses, non-profits and religious organizations; the allegations included requiring personal guarantees and upfront fees after representing that they would not make those demands, providing less funding than promised, debiting more than they said they would, unauthorised withdrawals, unfair collection practices that at times included threats of physical violence, and the weaponisation of confessions of judgment. The settlement order required vacating judgments against former customers and releasing liens on their property, and the case against the other defendants was described as ongoing. Each of those allegations converts into an advance check: does the offer state guarantees and fees before signature, does the disbursement equal what was promised, does the debit authority match the remittance schedule, and does the template contain a confession of judgment. Contract comes fourth: the counterparty's own template read through the four channels of the clause lesson. A vetting file does not guarantee an outcome and does not predict approval; it converts an unknown counterparty into verified, failed and unresolved facts, and the third state blocks exactly as the second does.
lessons.example: An eleven-check vetting file for a funder whose offer is on a merchant's desk. The checks and their results: registration current, verified, with the register's record dated; SBA participation as claimed, unresolved, because no participating-lender record was produced; filed enforcement and litigation history, verified with two items, one of which is an administrative order; the counterparty's own contract template read through the four channels, failed, because it contains a confession of judgment provision and a clause requiring disputes to be brought outside the state, both of which the state's sales-based financing chapter renders unenforceable; the debit authority compared with the remittance schedule, verified, because the debits in the template match the disclosed cadence; fee itemisation, failed, because two fees appear in the template that were absent from the offer summary; the governing disclosure items, failed, because the broker-compensation line required by the state's item list is missing from the offer document; complaint history across the federal and state consumer protection agencies, unresolved; two trade references, unresolved; evidence of any licence or registration for activity regulated in another state in which the merchant operates, unresolved; and the identity and authority of the individual who signs the offer, unresolved. The tally is four verified, three failed and four unresolved, so seven of eleven checks, or 63.64 percent, block the file. The cost of the exercise is small and computable: eleven checks at 25 minutes each is 275 minutes, 4.58 hours, which at $95.00 an hour is $435.42. The rule that makes the file useful is stated at the top: unresolved blocks in the same way a fail blocks, so the output is a yes, a no or a not yet, and the not-yet names what would move each unresolved row, which for this file is a participating-lender record, an agency complaint search with its date, two references contacted, one out-of-state registration record, and the signer's authority. The advisory line that accompanies it is deliberately narrow: the file does not say the counterparty is dishonest and does not predict that any agreement would fail; it records what was verified, what failed against the documents in hand, and what remains unknown.
lessons.question: A merchant wants to sign with a funder whose offer is attractive and whose vetting file shows four unresolved checks and one failed check. What is the correct output of the vetting process, and what does the advisor say?
lessons.answer: Not yet, with the unresolved rows named as blockers, because unresolved blocks exactly as a fail blocks; the advisor lists what would clear each row, in writing, and states separately what failed against the documents in hand, without alleging dishonesty or predicting an outcome.
lessons.distractor: Yes with caution, since the offer is attractive, the failures are documentary, and unresolved items are common in a market where records are incomplete, so the merchant should proceed while the advisor continues checking.
lessons.correction: Treating unresolved as a soft pass transfers the unknown to the merchant at the moment when the merchant has the least leverage, after signature. A failed row is a fact about a document; an unresolved row is a fact about the file, and both mean the advisor cannot yet describe what the merchant is agreeing to. The correct output is a not-yet with a clearance list, and the honest framing distinguishes what was verified from what was not found, since absence of a complaint record is not the same as absence of complaints. The same discipline applies to the offer itself: a contract containing a confession of judgment or an out-of-state forum clause is a finding about the document, whatever the counterparty's reputation.

depth.definitions: A vetting file is a dated set of checks, each with a source, a result and a note. The three results are verified, failed and unresolved, and unresolved is the absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence. Registration is permission to transact in a jurisdiction, granted by a regulator, and in Virginia it carries an initial fee of $1,000, an annual fee of $500 due by September 15, and automatic expiry by operation of law on non-payment, which makes registration status a dated fact rather than a permanent attribute. Participation in an SBA programme is likewise a status with published criteria for 7(a) lenders: the continuing ability to evaluate, process, close, disburse, service and liquidate small business loans; openness to the public and not being a financing subsidiary of an affiliate; continuing good character and reputation and the ethical requirements identified in 13 CFR part 120.140; and supervision and examination satisfactory to SBA or status as a Small Business Lending Company or Non-Federally Regulated Lender under SOP 50 56. An enforcement record is the public record of agency actions and court filings, read as allegations and dispositions rather than as conclusions. The contract template is the counterparty's own document, read for the four channels of amount, timing, responsibility and enforceability. A clearance list is the set of documents that would move an unresolved row. Scope: an advisor may not perform a regulator's function, may not defame a counterparty, and may not present a check as a legal opinion.
depth.mechanism: The file works because it converts a personal impression into a shared artifact that a merchant can hold. Four mechanisms do the work. First, the three-state rule prevents the common failure of collapsing ignorance into approval: because unresolved blocks like a fail, the default for an unknown is a not-yet rather than a yes with a note. Second, expired permission is a real category: a registration that lapses automatically on non-payment of an annual fee means that the question is not whether a firm was once registered but whether it is registered on the date it makes the offer. Third, programme claims are countable, so a claim of SBA participation can be tested against four published criteria instead of a logo, which is the difference between reading a marketing page and reading a standard. Fourth, an enforcement record is generative rather than merely cautionary: each allegation in a public matter suggests a document check the advisor can run in advance, which is why the FTC matter's allegations map onto the offer letter, the disbursement, the debit authority and the template. Running these four together produces a file whose value is not a verdict about character but a list of the things the merchant would otherwise learn after signing.
depth.secondExample: The same artifact built after a merchant has already signed becomes an audit and a remediation list rather than a gate, and the change in timing changes what matters. The checks are unchanged, but the output shifts from yes, no or not yet to a schedule of actions: a written demand for the missing disclosure item, a request for the payoff figures as of a stated date, a review of whether the debit authority matches the remittance actually being taken, and a dated note recording that unenforceable provisions in the template were identified and that the merchant was told to seek counsel before relying on them. A second contrast is a product sourced from an examined financial institution, where the permission question is answered by a supervisory regime rather than by a state register and the vetting file's rows change shape: no registration row, but rows for the programme criteria if a guarantee is claimed, for the contract template, and for the disclosure items where a state requires them. In both variants the three-state discipline and the clearance list transfer, which is what makes the file a production skill rather than a form.
depth.mistake: The first error is substituting a logo or a testimonial for a status check: a page that says an entity is a preferred partner of a programme is not a record that it participates in that programme. The second is treating a registration as permanent, when at least one state's statute makes it expire automatically if an annual fee is missed. The third is collapsing the three states, usually by marking an unanswered check as fine because nothing bad was found; absence of a complaint record is not evidence that no complaints exist, and the honest label is unresolved. The fourth is vetting the counterparty's marketing and not its template, which is where the confession of judgment, the out-of-state forum clause and the undisclosed fees live. The diagnostic is to read the file and count the three states aloud; a file with no unresolved rows has probably not been run carefully, and a file with no failed rows on a template review deserves a second look.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Build an eleven-check vetting file for one counterparty, using verified, failed and unresolved, and write the clearance list and the two-sentence advisory note. Model response: eleven rows with sources and dates, yielding four verified, three failed and four unresolved, so seven of eleven checks block the file, 63.64 percent; the failed rows are a confession of judgment provision and an out-of-state forum clause in the template, both unenforceable under the state chapter the file sits in, two fees present in the template but absent from the offer summary, and a missing broker-compensation line against the state's item list; the clearance list names a participating-lender record, a dated agency complaint search, two contacted references, one out-of-state registration record and the signer's written authority; the advisory note states that the file records what was verified and that it neither alleges dishonesty nor predicts an outcome; the effort is 11 checks times 25 minutes, 4.58 hours at $95.00 an hour, $435.42. Rubric: three points for eleven checks with sources and dates; three for correct use of the three states with unresolved treated as blocking; two for the clearance list naming documents; two for reading the counterparty's own template; two for an advisory note free of character claims and predictions. A file with unresolved rows marked as passes, or one that reaches a verdict about the counterparty's honesty, cannot pass.
depth.summary: A vetting file replaces an unknown counterparty with dated facts in three states, and the third state blocks. Permission is a dated fact rather than a permanent quality, programme claims are countable against published criteria, enforcement records generate document checks, and the counterparty's own template is the document where the enforceable and unenforceable terms actually live. What the artifact must not do is allege dishonesty, predict an outcome, or let an unknown pass as a yes, because the merchant's alternative is to discover all of it after signature.
